knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two same-layer nodes are locally equivalent when their terminal values or complete labeled successor signatures agree; merging them preserves the represented function.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Equivalence Detection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. The equivalence test is standard for a precisely specified ordered deterministic diagram model, but the treatment of weighted arcs and residual value functions depends on the weight-composition semantics and requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Recursive Subgraph Sharing
children.top_down_role: Reduction regimes based on reusable descendant structure.

assumptions_latex: The diagram is a finite acyclic decision graph.
Equivalent terminals and equivalent nonterminal signatures can be identified exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output contains one node per recursively computed signature and represents the same root function as the input.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Hash-consing nodes by recursively canonicalized child signatures is the standard construction for maximal DAG sharing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bottom-up hash-consing of identical residual subgraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Process nodes in reverse topological order. Assign each terminal a signature consisting of its terminal value. For a nonterminal \(u\), first replace every successor by its already chosen representative, then form \(\sigma(u)\) from the tested variable and the ordered list of labeled, weighted representative successors. Maintain a table \(H\). If \(H[\sigma(u)]\) exists, redirect all incoming arcs of \(u\) to that representative; otherwise set \(H[\sigma(u)]=u\). Return the representative of the original root after all reachable nodes have been processed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reverse-topological hash-consing merges nodes whose recursively canonicalized labeled subgraphs are identical, producing maximal sharing without changing root semantics.
knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Subgraph Sharing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. Reverse-topological hash-consing is plausible, but the claim of one node per signature and maximal semantic sharing requires a specified diagram model, canonical signature construction, and authoritative algorithm or canonicity reference.

children.title: Redundant Arc Reduction
children.top_down_role: Removal or consolidation of transitions that add no distinct representation.

assumptions_latex: The decision diagram is deterministic, and arc labels specify mutually distinguishable decisions.
Arc deletion is considered only for arcs reachable from the root.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deleting an arc is semantics-preserving exactly when it contributes no root-to-terminal assignment or no value beyond an identical parallel arc.

notation.meaning: Set of represented completions using arc \(e\).
Tail, decision label, weight, and head signature of \(e\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Unreachable arcs and duplicate parallel arcs are elementary semantic redundancies in deterministic decision DAGs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact removal criteria for unreachable or duplicate arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An arc \(e\) is redundant if either \(C(e)=\varnothing\), or there exists a distinct parallel arc \(e'\) with \(\tau(e)=\tau(e')\). In the first case, no represented root-to-terminal completion uses \(e\); in the second, every completion and accumulated value obtained through \(e\) is also obtained through \(e'\). Deleting \(e\) therefore preserves the represented feasible assignments and objective values. Deleting an arc that has a unique decision label and satisfies \(C(e)\ne\varnothing\) is not justified by this local criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc may be deleted when it supports no completion or exactly duplicates a parallel labeled transition; a uniquely contributing feasible arc is not redundant.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Arc Reduction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. The criterion mixes set-valued and objective-valued semantics, while the definitions of completion contribution, parallel-arc identity, and accumulated values are model-dependent. A source specifying those semantics is required.

children.title: Redundant Node Reduction
children.top_down_role: Removal or bypass of nodes that add no distinct continuation structure.

assumptions_latex: The diagram is a finite rooted decision DAG.
Bypassing a node composes incoming and outgoing labels and weights according to the diagram semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Removing an unreachable node or bypassing a semantically neutral unary node preserves the represented root function.

notation.meaning: Set of nodes reachable from the root.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Reachability deletion and neutral unary-node bypass are standard graph and decision-diagram reductions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Removal of unreachable and semantically neutral unary nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: First compute the reachable set \(R\) and delete every node outside \(R\). Next, if a nonterminal node \(u\) has exactly one outgoing arc \((u,v)\), and the decision at \(u\) is forced on every partial assignment reaching \(u\), redirect each incoming arc \((p,u)\) to \(v\). Compose its label and weight with those of \((u,v)\), then delete \(u\). Repeat until neither rule applies. The output is the remaining root-reachable diagram; terminals are never bypassed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete unreachable nodes and repeatedly bypass a forced unary node by composing its incident transitions; these operations preserve all represented completions and values.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Node Reduction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. Unreachable-node deletion is elementary, but bypassing a forced unary node is valid only under precisely defined label and weight composition rules. Those rules and the preservation claim need an authoritative source.

children.title: Arc-Induced Node Redundancy
children.top_down_role: Node redundancies exposed after transition removal or consolidation.

assumptions_latex: A node becomes unary only after semantics-preserving arc deletions.
The remaining outgoing decision is forced for every partial assignment reaching that node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Arc reduction creates a valid node-reduction opportunity, and bypassing the resulting unary node preserves the represented function.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Deleting redundant transitions can lower outdegree and expose forced unary nodes suitable for bypass.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node redundancy exposed by prior arc deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D'\) be obtained from \(D\) by deleting redundant outgoing arcs of a reachable nonterminal node \(u\). If \(|\delta_D^+(u)|>1\) but \(|\delta_{D'}^+(u)|=1\), then arc reduction has exposed a unary node. When the sole remaining transition is forced for every state reaching \(u\), the test at \(u\) carries no residual choice. Redirecting each incoming arc through that transition, with the prescribed label and weight composition, eliminates \(u\) while preserving the root residual function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Removing redundant arcs can make a node unary; if its remaining transition is forced, the node can then be bypassed without changing semantics.
knowledge_statements.title: Arc-Induced Node Redundancy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. The property fits the leaf, but whether a unary node is bypassable depends on the decision-diagram semantics and the exact composition of incoming and outgoing transitions.

children.title: Reduction Order Effects
children.top_down_role: Structural effects of applying arc-level versus node-level reductions in different orders.

assumptions_latex: Each individual arc or node reduction preserves the represented function.
Applying one rule may create new instances of another rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A single ordered pass can depend on rule order, whereas iteration to a common fixed point is order-independent only under confluence.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Interacting rewrite rules can expose one another, so one-pass normal forms may depend on scheduling unless confluence is established.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduling boundary for interacting arc and node reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(D\to_A D_A\) can expose a node reduction and \(D\to_N D_N\) can expose an arc reduction. Then applying each rule only once may yield diagrams of different sizes because a later-created opportunity is not revisited. Repeated fair application terminates when every step strictly decreases the finite number of arcs or nodes. However, termination and semantic preservation alone do not imply a unique reduced graph: order independence requires confluence, namely that whenever \(D\to_A D_A\) and \(D\to_N D_N\), both descendants reduce to isomorphic normal forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interacting reductions may expose new opportunities, so one-pass results can depend on order; a unique fixed point additionally requires confluence, not merely termination.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduction Order Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source or counterexample is cited. The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, but the asserted interaction of these particular reductions and the stated isomorphic-normal-form confluence condition require a formal rewrite model and supporting source.

children.title: Minimum-Size Diagram Criteria
children.top_down_role: Size criteria used to compare equivalent diagram representations.

assumptions_latex: The variable order is fixed and every nonterminal layer tests its prescribed variable.
The diagram is deterministic, complete on its reachable residual states, and uses canonical terminals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The diagram is minimum among diagrams respecting that order exactly when distinct reachable nodes denote distinct residual functions and no node is semantically redundant.

notation.meaning: Set of reachable nodes in layer \(i\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Fixed-order canonical decision diagrams contain exactly one node for each distinct reachable residual function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-order deterministic diagram minimality via distinct residual functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each layer \(i\), associate with every reachable node \(u\in V_i\) its residual function \(F_u\) on the unassigned variables. A reduced diagram is minimum-size among deterministic diagrams using the same variable order if and only if, in every layer, \(F_u\ne F_v\) for all distinct \(u,v\in V_i\), and no nonterminal node has a semantically vacuous test that can be bypassed. Under these conditions every equivalent fixed-order diagram requires at least one node for each distinct reachable residual function, so its layer sizes and total node count cannot be smaller.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed order, a deterministic diagram is minimum when each reachable residual function has one node and no tested variable is semantically vacuous.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Size Diagram Criteria

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited for this nontrivial minimality theorem. Its validity depends on the exact decision-diagram class, permitted skipped variables, terminal and arc semantics, and the size measure; the present hypotheses do not fix these sufficiently.

children.title: Reduction versus Global Minimality
children.top_down_role: Distinction between locally irreducible diagrams plus globally minimum representations.

assumptions_latex: All local reductions preserve the represented function.
The comparison class may include diagrams with different variable orders or richer node and arc representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local irreducibility does not certify global minimum size over the enlarged representation class.

notation.meaning: Diagram reduced under the chosen local rules.
Allowed comparison class of equivalent diagrams.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Decision-diagram size can vary sharply with variable order, so fixed-order reduction is not unrestricted global minimization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes local normal form from unrestricted diagram minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) contain no mergeable equivalent nodes, redundant arcs, or bypassable nodes under a specified local reduction system. This establishes only that \(D\) is a normal form for those rules. If \(\mathcal C\) permits another variable order, additional arc labels, skipped variables, or alternative decomposition structure, there may exist \(D'\in\mathcal C\) representing the same function with \(|V(D')|<|V(D)|\). Therefore local reduction certifies global minimum size only when a separate canonicity or lower-bound theorem covers the entire comparison class \(\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally irreducible diagram need not be globally smallest when alternative variable orders or representation structures are allowed; global minimality needs an additional theorem.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduction versus Global Minimality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source or explicit counterexample is cited. The distinction between local irreducibility and global minimality is appropriate, but the claim that a smaller equivalent diagram may exist over the enlarged class needs authoritative variable-ordering evidence or a specifically sourced counterexample.

children.title: Variable Ordering
children.top_down_role: Static and adaptive ordering regimes that govern exposed state, diagram width, and approximation quality.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Variable Ordering

assumptions_latex: The variables are \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), each with a finite domain.
The order is selected before compilation and remains unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every root-to-terminal path respects one fixed permutation of the variables.

notation.meaning: A permutation of the variable indices.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: A static decision-diagram order is a permutation fixed before construction and respected monotonically on every path.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed permutation chosen before exact diagram compilation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A static variable ordering is a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) fixed before decision-diagram compilation. Every nonterminal node in layer \(L_i\) tests \(x_{\pi(i)}\), and every root-to-terminal path visits tested variables in increasing layer index, possibly skipping layers only if the diagram formalism permits skipped irrelevant variables. The permutation \(\pi\) is not changed in response to intermediate widths, node counts, or compilation states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Static ordering fixes one variable permutation before compilation, and all root-to-terminal paths respect it without feedback-driven changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Static Variable Ordering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. The definition is plausible for layered ordered decision diagrams, but static ordering does not universally require every layer to correspond to one tested variable; the skipped-variable convention and diagram formalism need sourced specification.

children.title: Adaptive Variable Ordering
children.top_down_role: Ordering choices revised using observed compilation or search behavior.

assumptions_latex: Compilation exposes measurable partial-diagram states after selected stages.
Reordering preserves the function represented by the already compiled portion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns an exact diagram while allowing later variable choices to depend on observed compilation states.

notation.meaning: Feedback policy selecting the next variable.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Adaptive ordering selects future variables from feedback observed during incremental compilation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online choice of future variables during incremental compilation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(U_0=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) and an exact root frontier. At stage \(k\), measure the current state \(s_k\), choose \(x_k=\Phi(U_k,s_k)\), expand every frontier state on \(x_k\), and apply exact equivalence and redundancy reductions. Set \(U_{k+1}=U_k\setminus\{x_k\}\). Stop when \(U_k=\varnothing\) or every frontier state is terminal, and return the reduced diagram. The policy may revise only unprocessed positions; it must not discard feasible completions or merge inequivalent states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive ordering repeatedly chooses the next unprocessed variable from current width or state feedback while exact expansion and reduction preserve the represented problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Variable Ordering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. The algorithm fits adaptive ordering, but exactness under online selection, frontier expansion, early termination, and reduction depends on an explicitly defined compilation model and preservation invariant.

children.title: Dynamic Variable Reordering
children.top_down_role: Changes to variable positions during diagram construction or use.

assumptions_latex: An exact decision diagram has already been constructed or partially constructed.
A semantics-preserving adjacent-level exchange operation is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted exchanges change the current order and diagram structure without changing the represented function.

notation.meaning: Diagram obtained by exchanging adjacent levels \(i\) and \(i+1\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Dynamic reordering changes an existing ordered diagram through semantics-preserving level exchanges and reduction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantics-preserving reordering of an existing diagram.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a diagram \(D\) with current order \(\pi\), select an adjacent position \(i\), construct \(S_i(D)\) by exchanging the tests at levels \(i\) and \(i+1\), and reduce the affected subgraph exactly. Accept the exchange according to a stated rule, such as \(M(S_i(D))<M(D)\), then update \(D\) and \(\pi\); otherwise retain the previous pair. Continue until a complete sweep accepts no exchange or a prescribed work budget is exhausted. Return the best exact diagram encountered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic reordering exchanges levels in an existing diagram, exactly rebuilds affected subgraphs, and retains changes according to a size metric or work budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Variable Reordering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. Dynamic adjacent-level exchange is standard in some ordered decision-diagram frameworks, but the construction of the exchanged subgraph and its semantic preservation require an authoritative algorithmic reference.

children.title: Ordering Feedback Signals
children.top_down_role: Width, state diversity, reduction potential, plus search information used for ordering choices.

assumptions_latex: Every candidate signal is computed from the current exact partial diagram.
The ordering policy uses signals only to rank admissible next choices or reorderings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The signal vector is valid feedback when it is observable before the decision and does not alter diagram semantics.

notation.meaning: Number of nodes created and retained at stage \(k\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Width, node growth, merge rate, and reduction yield are natural observable statistics for feedback-driven diagram ordering.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observable statistics used by feedback-driven ordering policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At compilation stage \(k\), an ordering feedback signal is a statistic measurable before the next ordering action and derived from the current diagram state. A representative vector is \(s_k=(w_k,n_k,g_k,r_k,c_k)\), where \(w_k\) is frontier width, \(n_k\) is retained node count, \(g_k=n_k-n_{k-1}\) is node growth, \(r_k\) is the fraction of generated nodes or arcs removed by exact reduction, and \(c_k\) is measured construction cost. Such signals guide ranking but do not themselves authorize inexact deletion or merging.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordering feedback consists of observable statistics such as frontier width, node growth, reduction yield, and construction cost; signals guide choices without changing exact semantics.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordering Feedback Signals

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. The definition fits the leaf, but the proposed feedback vector and reduction-yield statistic are heuristic choices rather than a canonical definition and require a source establishing their use in feedback-driven ordering.

children.title: Reordering Overhead Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where reordering cost outweighs diagram-size or search benefits.

assumptions_latex: At layer \(i\), the current and proposed variable orders induce remaining compilation costs \(C_i(\pi)\) and \(C_i(\pi')\).
Changing from \(\pi\) to \(\pi'\) costs \(R_i(\pi,\pi')\) units in the same resource measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi'\) is beneficial exactly when \(R_i(\pi,\pi')<C_i(\pi)-C_i(\pi')\).

notation.meaning: Compilation resource cost from layer i onward under order pi
Resource cost of changing orders at layer i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amortized boundary for dynamic reordering under a common resource measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a compilation layer \(i\) and measure both diagram construction and reordering in one resource, such as elementary operations or elapsed time. Let \(C_i(\pi)\) and \(C_i(\pi')\) be the costs of completing compilation under the current and proposed orders, and let \(R_i(\pi,\pi')\) be the reordering overhead. The total costs are respectively \(C_i(\pi)\) and \(R_i(\pi,\pi')+C_i(\pi')\). Hence reordering has positive net benefit precisely when \[R_i(\pi,\pi')<C_i(\pi)-C_i(\pi').\] Equality is the break-even boundary; reversing the inequality makes reordering overhead dominate its downstream saving.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reordering is worthwhile only when its overhead is smaller than the remaining compilation cost it saves.
knowledge_statements.title: Reordering Overhead Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The break-even inequality is algebraically correct once benefit means lower total cost in a common resource measure, but no cited source supports this instantiated cost model. It is a decision condition, not a complexity bound.

assumptions_latex: The finite-domain model has variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and a primal interaction graph \(G=(V,E)\).
An edge joins variables occurring together in some constraint or objective term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The elimination order returned by repeated minimum fill is a problem-structure variable order.

notation.meaning: Number of missing neighbor edges created by eliminating v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete static ordering heuristic based on the model interaction graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct the primal interaction graph \(G=(V,E)\), with one vertex per variable and an edge between variables appearing together in a constraint or objective term. Initialize \(G_1=G\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), compute for every remaining vertex \(v\) the fill count \(\phi_{G_i}(v)\), equal to the number of absent edges among its current neighbors. Select \(v_i\in\operatorname*{argmin}_v\phi_{G_i}(v)\), resolving ties by a fixed deterministic rule; make its neighbors a clique and delete \(v_i\) to obtain \(G_{i+1}\). Output \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) as the decision-diagram variable order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly eliminate the variable creating the fewest interaction-graph fill edges, using the elimination sequence as the diagram order.
knowledge_statements.title: Problem-Structure Ordering Heuristics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Minimum fill is a recognizable graph-elimination heuristic, but no source establishes its use or the elimination-sequence direction as a decision-diagram variable order; some compilation conventions require the reverse order.

children.title: Decision-Diagram Exactness Conditions
children.top_down_role: Certificate families distinguishing exact solution-space and objective representation from approximate compilation.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Exact Decision Diagrams

assumptions_latex: Each root-to-terminal path of \(D\) has one label in every variable domain.
The label map \(\lambda\) sends a path to its complete assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed bidirectional membership test certifies \(\lambda(P(D))=F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-language certificate for exact representation of the feasible solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq X_1\times\cdots\times X_n\) be the feasible assignments and let \(P(D)\) be the root-to-terminal paths of a layered decision diagram \(D\). A solution-space exactness certificate consists of two verifiable claims: soundness, \(\lambda(p)\in F\) for every \(p\in P(D)\), and completeness, for every \(x\in F\) there exists \(p\in P(D)\) with \(\lambda(p)=x\). Together they establish \[\lambda(P(D))=F.\] If path labels are unique assignments, the certificate may additionally establish a bijection, but uniqueness is not required for solution-space exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diagram is solution-space exact when every path is feasible and every feasible assignment is represented by a path.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Space Exactness Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The soundness-and-completeness characterization is mathematically coherent and the certificate content kind fits, but the record supplies no inspectable citation for this decision-diagram exactness formulation.

children.title: State-Model Exactness Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates concerning preservation of relevant history within recursive states.

assumptions_latex: Prefixes are taken at the same layer and therefore have the same unassigned variables.
The state map \(q_i\) is computable from each layer-\(i\) prefix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated completion and continuation-value equalities certify that \(q_i\) is an exact state model.

notation.meaning: Feasible suffix completions after prefix p
Continuation objective contribution for suffix y after p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Future-equivalence certificate for a layered state model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every layer \(i\), let \(K_i(p)\) be the feasible suffix assignments extending a prefix \(p\), and let \(h_i(p,y)\) be the objective contribution still attributable to suffix \(y\). A state-model exactness certificate verifies that whenever \(q_i(p)=q_i(p')\), one has \[K_i(p)=K_i(p')\quad\text{and}\quad h_i(p,y)=h_i(p',y)\ \text{for every }\ y\in K_i(p).\] It also verifies that transitions from \(q_i(p)\) under each next-variable value produce \(q_{i+1}(p,y_i)\). These checks certify that the state retains all future feasibility and continuation-objective information required by exact compilation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal states must have identical feasible continuations, continuation values, and successor-state behavior.
knowledge_statements.title: State-Model Exactness Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The future-equivalence idea fits the container, but the sufficiency of the listed tests depends on the compilation and objective conventions. The transition expression also uses the next value y_i without defining its domain or distinguishing it from a suffix y.

children.title: Merging Exactness Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates concerning safe consolidation of diagram nodes or states.

assumptions_latex: Only nodes in the same layer are eligible for merging.
Each node represents the set of prefixes reaching it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A merge satisfying future congruence preserves the diagram's feasible path language and continuation objectives.

notation.meaning: Feasible suffix language from node u
Continuation value of suffix y from node u

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness test for merging two nodes at a common layer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\) and \(v\) be nodes in the same layer. An exact merging certificate verifies future congruence: \[L(u)=L(v),\qquad c(u,y)=c(v,y)\ \text{for every }\ y\in L(u).\] For each admissible next label, it further verifies that the successors of \(u\) and \(v\) are identical or are themselves related by the certified congruence. The merged node \(m(u,v)\) inherits the common outgoing labeled transitions and continuation values, while all incoming arcs of \(u\) and \(v\) are redirected to it. Under these checks, merging changes neither represented complete assignments nor their objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two same-layer nodes can be merged exactly when their labeled futures and all continuation values agree congruently.
knowledge_statements.title: Merging Exactness Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed future-congruence certificate is plausible, but no source supports the stated merge construction or establishes that its conditions cover all arc-label, accumulated-cost, and terminal semantics needed for exactness.

children.title: Joint State–Merge Certification
children.top_down_role: Coordinated certification of state adequacy plus merge validity.

assumptions_latex: A state-model certificate holds at every layer.
Every performed merge satisfies the merging certificate relative to the certified states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The compiled quotient diagram represents exactly the feasible assignments and their objective values.

notation.meaning: Diagram obtained by certified state merging

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compositional certificate combining state sufficiency and merge congruence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be compiled from a state map satisfying the state-model exactness certificate. Let \(\sim\) be a same-layer equivalence relation such that every identified pair satisfies the merging exactness certificate, including successor congruence and continuation-value equality. The joint certificate records these facts for every reachable state and every quotient class. It then certifies \[\lambda(P(D/{\sim}))=\lambda(P(D))=F\] and, for every quotient path \(p\), equality between its represented objective value and that of any corresponding path in \(D\). Thus the quotient preserves both the solution space and objective representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact states plus congruent exact merges jointly certify preservation of feasible assignments and their objective values.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint State–Merge Certification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits the leaf, but the quotient exactness conclusion requires a sourced compositional theorem. The claimed correspondence between quotient paths and paths in D is not formally introduced or justified by the stated hypotheses alone.

children.title: Certificate Coverage Gaps
children.top_down_role: Exactness risks not resolved by state-model or merge-specific evidence.

assumptions_latex: A proposed certificate checks only explicitly listed state or merge predicates.
Unverified feasibility, transition, reachability, or objective predicates may affect complete paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure to cover any required predicate leaves exactness uncertified, even if every checked predicate passes.

notation.meaning: Predicates actually checked by the certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary of partial state-and-merge certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be the set of feasibility, transition, reachability, and objective predicates required by the selected exactness theorem, and let \(C\subseteq R\) be those actually checked. If \(R\setminus C\ne\varnothing\), passing all checks in \(C\) does not certify exactness. Concretely, two prefixes may have the same feasible suffix set and identical successor structure but different accumulated objective offsets. Merging them while storing only one offset preserves the feasible path language yet assigns an incorrect value to paths from the other prefix. Thus objective coverage cannot be inferred from feasibility-and-transition coverage; every predicate used by the exactness conclusion must be certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unchecked exactness predicates remain genuine gaps; feasibility-equivalent states can still require different objective information.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Coverage Gaps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coverage-gap principle and objective-offset example are coherent and the failure-boundary kind fits. However, the required predicate set R is delegated to an unspecified exactness theorem, and neither that theorem nor a supporting source is cited.

assumptions_latex: Every complete assignment represented by the diagram has at least one root-to-terminal path.
The optimization objective is \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The path-value identity certifies exact objective representation; combined with solution-space exactness, diagram optimization equals optimization over \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive path-weight certificate for objective preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a layered diagram whose arcs have weights \(w(a)\), and define the value of a root-to-terminal path \(p\) by \(W(p)=\sum_{a\in p}w(a)\). An objective-representation exactness certificate verifies \[W(p)=f(\lambda(p))\quad\text{for every }\ p\in P(D).\] If multiple paths encode one assignment, the identity must hold for every such path. When \(\lambda(P(D))=F\), this certificate yields \[\min_{p\in P(D)}W(p)=\min_{x\in F}f(x),\] with \(\min\) replaced consistently by \(\max\) for maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every path weight must equal the objective of its encoded assignment; then diagram and original optima coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Representation Exactness Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive path-value certificate is standard in form and fits the container, but it has no citation. The optimum equality also needs F and P(D) to be nonempty or an explicit extended-value convention for minima over empty sets.

children.title: Primal-Dual Diagram Approximation Family
children.top_down_role: Limited-width over- and under-approximations used for dual bounds, primal bounds, propagation, and exact search.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Relaxed Decision Diagrams; Restricted Decision Diagrams

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Decision Diagrams for Discrete Optimization: A Survey of Recent Advances
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Approximate DD Compilation; Bounds and Search; CP Propagation
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Decision Diagrams for Discrete Optimization: A Survey of Recent Advances

children.title: Relaxed Decision Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Over-approximating diagrams produced through state aggregation or relaxation-aware refinement.

assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem and diagram paths encode complete assignments.
Nodes selected for merging lie in the same layer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Union-based merging produces a relaxation; with non-overestimating path costs, its shortest path is a valid lower bound.

notation.meaning: Suffix assignments admitted from node u
Relaxed merge of nodes u and v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Union merge for relaxed diagrams in finite-domain minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For same-layer nodes \(u\) and \(v\), a relaxed state merge replaces them by a node \(u\sqcup v\) whose admitted suffix language contains their union: \[L(u)\cup L(v)\subseteq L(u\sqcup v).\] All incoming prefixes formerly reaching \(u\) or \(v\) reach the merged node, and outgoing transitions are retained or enlarged so that no previously represented complete assignment is removed. Consequently the resulting diagram \(D^R\) satisfies \(F\subseteq\lambda(P(D^R))\). If every relaxed path value is no greater than the objective of its encoded assignment, then \(\min_{p\in P(D^R)}W(p)\leq\min_{x\in F}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxed merge unions or enlarges node futures, preserving all feasible assignments and potentially adding paths that yield a minimization lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed State Merging

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Union-based relaxed merging is plausible, but no decision-diagram source supports the precise relaxation and cost convention. The bound condition invokes W, f, lambda, and P(D) without fully defining them, and f may be undefined on added infeasible assignments.

children.title: Merge Candidate Selection
children.top_down_role: Identification of node groups eligible for relaxed merging.

assumptions_latex: A diagram layer exceeds its prescribed width.
The eligible same-layer merge pairs form a finite nonempty set \(M\).
A deterministic score \(s:M\to\mathbb{R}\) ranks candidate pairs, with lower values preferred.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a layer satisfying the width limit unless no eligible pair remains.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy pair selection for enforcing a relaxed-diagram width limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a layer \(U\), width limit \(W\), eligibility relation \(M\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in U,\ u\ne v\}\), and score \(s\), repeat while \(|U|>W\): select \[
\{u,v\}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{e\in M}s(e),
\] break ties by a fixed rule, replace \(u,v\) by their relaxed merge \(u\sqcup v\), update affected transitions, candidate pairs, and scores, and discard pairs containing removed nodes. Stop successfully when \(|U|\leq W\); stop with failure if \(M=\varnothing\) first. Output the modified layer together with the ordered merge log for reproducibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly choose the lowest-scored eligible pair, merge it, and update candidates until the layer meets its width limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Merge Candidate Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The greedy selection procedure fits the algorithm leaf, but it lacks a source and does not specify the domain of W. It should test whether the updated candidate set is empty before taking an argmin at every iteration.

children.title: Merge Scoring
children.top_down_role: Priority measures for comparing candidate merges.

assumptions_latex: Each eligible pair has finitely many real-valued merge features.
Feature scales are strictly positive and weights are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The weighted normalized sum defines an auditable scalar ranking of merge candidates.

notation.meaning: Positive calibration scale for feature j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic normalized multi-feature score for relaxed merge ranking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d_j(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,k\) quantify predicted consequences of merging eligible nodes \(u,v\), with smaller values preferred. Given locations \(\mu_j\), positive scales \(\sigma_j\), and weights \(\alpha_j\geq0\) satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j=1\), define \[s(u,v)=\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j\frac{d_j(u,v)-\mu_j}{\sigma_j}.\] Candidate pairs are ranked in increasing order of \(s\), with a fixed secondary key for ties. The feature definitions, calibration parameters, weights, and tie rule are part of the scoring specification and must be recorded to make selection reproducible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A merge score combines normalized impact features with recorded nonnegative weights and ranks candidates from lowest to highest.
knowledge_statements.title: Merge Scoring

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalized weighted score is internally coherent and fits the scoring leaf, but it is a noncanonical heuristic specification with no cited decision-diagram or methodological source supporting the selected score family.

children.title: Score Calibration Regimes
children.top_down_role: Normalization plus weighting choices across layers, widths, or state types.

assumptions_latex: For each calibration regime, feature samples are finite and each retained feature has positive scale.
Regime membership is determined before candidate scores are compared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scores are comparable within a regime; cross-regime comparison requires a shared calibration map.

notation.meaning: Calibration regime, such as a fixed layer or compilation phase

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Within-regime normalization condition for comparable merge scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition score evaluations into regimes \(r\), for example by layer, width range, or compilation phase. For feature \(j\) in regime \(r\), choose a location \(\mu_{jr}\) and scale \(\sigma_{jr}>0\) from a fixed reference sample, and use \(z_{jr}(u,v)=(d_j(u,v)-\mu_{jr})/\sigma_{jr}\). A valid within-regime calibration holds the feature definitions, reference sample, normalization rule, and weights fixed while candidates are compared. Scores from distinct regimes may be compared only if a common reference distribution or an explicitly fitted monotone mapping places them on one scale; otherwise their numerical ordering has no prescribed meaning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalize candidates against a fixed reference within each regime, and compare different regimes only through an explicit common calibration.
knowledge_statements.title: Score Calibration Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The within-regime normalization condition fits the leaf, but no source supports the proposed regimes or the cross-regime criterion. An unspecified fitted monotone mapping alone does not necessarily establish meaningful comparability across regimes.

children.title: Misleading Merge Scores
children.top_down_role: Scoring regimes that poorly predict bound quality or downstream diagram structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Misleading Merge Scores
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of an uncalibrated merge score to predict relaxation-bound degradation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a maximization problem and a relaxed decision diagram with upper bound \(U(D)\). For a candidate merge \(M\), define its true degradation by \(\Delta(M)=U(D_M)-U(D)\), where \(D_M\) is the diagram after merging. If the selection rule minimizes a surrogate score \(s(M)\), that score is misleading whenever candidates \(M_1,M_2\) satisfy \(s(M_1)<s(M_2)\) but \(\Delta(M_1)>\Delta(M_2)\). Thus score ordering alone gives no bound-quality guarantee unless the calibration implication \(s(M_1)\le s(M_2)\Rightarrow\Delta(M_1)\le\Delta(M_2)\) is established on the applicable candidate class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A merge score is misleading when it prefers a merge that worsens the relaxation bound more than a rejected alternative.
assumptions_latex: \(D_M\) remains a valid relaxation for every candidate \(M\).
\(U(D)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s(M_1)<s(M_2)\) need not imply \(\Delta(M_1)\le\Delta(M_2)\).

notation.meaning: upper bound supplied by relaxed diagram D
diagram obtained after candidate merge M

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but no inspectable source supports this decision-diagram-specific calibration claim. A reversed pair establishes a misleading ranking, but full order-preserving calibration is sufficient rather than necessary for every possible bound-quality guarantee.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed-Diagram Width Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Layerwise width enforcement by validity-preserving state merges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a layered relaxed decision diagram \(D=(V,A)\), width limit \(W\ge1\), valid merge operator \(\mu\), and candidate score \(s\). Process layers in topological order. While a layer \(V_i\) satisfies \(|V_i|>W\), select an admissible pair minimizing \(s\), replace it by \(m=\mu(u,v)\), and redirect incident arcs according to the merge certificate. Remove duplicate or unreachable structure after each layer. Stop when every layer has width at most \(W\), and output \(D'\). If every application of \(\mu\) overapproximates both merged states and their transitions, then \(D'\) retains every feasible solution represented by \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly merge admissible states until each layer meets the width cap; valid merges preserve the relaxation’s feasible-solution containment.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is finite, layered, and acyclic.
\(W\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}\).
\(\mu\) has a valid local overapproximation certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_i|V_i(D')|\le W\) and \(\mathcal{X}(D)\subseteq\mathcal{X}(D')\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits width control, and the procedure is coherent. Its containment conclusion depends on a precise merge and arc-redirection validity theorem for which no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Decision-Diagram Relaxation Bound Validity
children.top_down_role: Certificate families for solution-space containment, value compatibility, and valid dual-bound extraction.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Decision Diagrams for Discrete Optimization: A Survey of Recent Advances
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Relaxed DD definitions; merged states; dual bounds
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Decision Diagrams for Discrete Optimization: A Survey of Recent Advances

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Space Containment Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local state-set certificate that every feasible assignment has a relaxed-diagram path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_i\) be the exact states reachable before decision layer \(i\), let \(R(v)\) label each relaxed node \(v\), and let \(\tau_i(s,a)\) be the exact transition. A containment certificate consists of \(s_0\in R(r)\) and, for every feasible transition \(s\mapsto\tau_i(s,a)\) with \(s\in R(u)\), an arc \((u,a,v)\) satisfying \(\tau_i(s,a)\in R(v)\). Terminal acceptance must contain every reachable feasible terminal state. These locally checkable inclusions certify that every feasible decision sequence labels a root-to-terminal path of the relaxed diagram.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initial-state, transition, and terminal inclusions certify that every feasible solution is represented by a relaxed root-to-terminal path.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau_i\) exactly describes feasible state transitions.
The diagram is finite and layered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{X}(D_R)\).

notation.meaning: exact-state set represented by relaxed node v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the leaf, but no source supports the proposed local certificate. The conclusion also uses D_R and X(D_R) without explicitly defining them, while S_i is introduced but not integrated into the certificate conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Merge-Operator Validity Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local sufficient conditions for a state merge to preserve relaxation containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For relaxed nodes \(u,v\) at one layer, a validity certificate for \(m=\mu(u,v)\) provides \(R(u)\cup R(v)\subseteq R(m)\). It also verifies that for every label \(a\) and every exact state \(s\in R(u)\cup R(v)\) for which \(\tau_i(s,a)\) is feasible, the merged node has an arc \((m,a,w)\) with \(\tau_i(s,a)\in R(w)\). Redirecting incoming arcs of \(u,v\) to \(m\) and using these certified outgoing arcs cannot remove a previously represented feasible root-to-terminal decision sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A merge is valid when its state set covers both inputs and its outgoing arcs cover every feasible successor transition.
assumptions_latex: \(u\) and \(v\) belong to the same layer.
Node labels denote sets of exact states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{X}(D)\subseteq\mathcal{X}(D_{\mu(u,v)})\).

notation.meaning: exact-state set represented by node q
exact successor under decision label a

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the leaf, but the source-free local conditions only explicitly preserve feasible exact transitions. They do not justify containment of every assignment represented by the original relaxed diagram, as asserted by X(D) subseteq X(D_mu), without an additional path-preservation hypothesis or a narrower feasible-solution conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Path-Value Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-bound certificate for maximization from relaxed path containment and arc domination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximization problem with objective \(f(x)\), let \(D_R\) be an acyclic relaxed diagram with arc weights \(c(a)\). A path-value certificate supplies, for every feasible solution \(x\), a representing root-to-terminal path \(p_x\) and verifies \(f(x)\le C(p_x):=\sum_{a\in p_x}c(a)\). Computing \(U=\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}(D_R)}C(p)\) by an acyclic longest-path recursion then gives \(f(x)\le U\) for every feasible \(x\). Hence \(U\) is a valid relaxation upper bound; inequalities reverse for minimization lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Containment plus path weights dominating feasible objectives certifies that the best relaxed path is a valid optimization bound.
assumptions_latex: \(D_R\) is finite and acyclic.
Every feasible solution has a representing path.
Certified arc weights dominate the corresponding objective contributions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{x\in\mathcal{F}}f(x)\le\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}(D_R)}C(p)=U\).

notation.meaning: root-to-terminal paths of the relaxed diagram
sum of arc weights on path p
