children.title: Decision-Diagram Compilation Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity regimes determined by encoding, state growth, structural parameters, and variable order.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Size Compilation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive bound for layered finite-state compilation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an \(n\)-stage decision-diagram compiler whose layer width is at most \(p(L)\), where \(L\) is the binary input length and \(p\) is a polynomial. Suppose every state has at most \(d(L)\) outgoing labels and each successor and arc value is computed in \(q(L)\) time, with \(d\) and \(q\) polynomial. Then the diagram has at most \((n+1)p(L)\) nodes and \(np(L)d(L)\) arcs. Layerwise compilation takes \(O(np(L)d(L)q(L))\) time and \(O(p(L)d(L))\) working space, excluding stored output; hence compilation is polynomial in \(L\) when \(n\) is polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial layer width, branching, transition cost, and stage count yield polynomial diagram size and compilation time.
assumptions_latex: \(n,p(L),d(L),q(L)\) are polynomially bounded in input length \(L\).
Compilation processes each generated state-label pair once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Diagram size and compilation time are polynomial in \(L\).
review_flags: The supplied polynomial-algorithm locator is not specific to decision-diagram compilation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The node, arc, and time counts are plausible in the stated layerwise model, but the working-space claim requires bounds for state representation, successor computation, and duplicate detection. No decision-diagram compilation source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudopolynomial State-Space Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compilation indexed by a numerically bounded dynamic-programming state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an \(n\)-stage integer dynamic program whose reachable state at each layer lies in \(\{0,1,\ldots,U\}\), with at most \(d\) decisions per state and constant-time arithmetic on values of magnitude polynomial in \(U\). Direct exact decision-diagram compilation creates at most \((n+1)(U+1)\) nodes and \(nd(U+1)\) arcs, and runs in \(O(ndU)\) arithmetic operations. This is polynomial in the numeric value \(U\) but may be exponential in its encoding length \(\lceil\log_2(U+1)\rceil\); it is therefore pseudopolynomial rather than polynomial in the binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state range of size U gives an O(ndU) compiler, which is pseudopolynomial because U may be exponential in its bit length.
assumptions_latex: Each layer has at most \(U+1\) reachable integer states.
Every state has at most \(d\) outgoing decisions.
Successor computation uses constant-time arithmetic in the stated model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact compilation uses \(O(ndU)\) operations and may be exponential in \(\log U\).
review_flags: A decision-diagram or dynamic-programming source supporting this precise resource model is needed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pseudopolynomial interpretation is standard, but the exact operation bound should be O(nd(U+1)) unless U is explicitly assumed positive. The unit-cost arithmetic model and compilation count also lack a supporting source.

children.title: Exponential-Width Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem families or orderings requiring exponentially many states within at least one layer.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential-Width Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-subproblem lower bound for exact ordered diagrams.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a variable ordering and a layer \(i\). Declare two feasible prefixes equivalent when they admit exactly the same feasible suffixes with the same suffix objective contributions. Any exact deterministic decision diagram must place inequivalent prefixes in distinct nodes at layer \(i\); otherwise merging them would identify different residual subproblems and alter feasibility or path values. Therefore, if an instance family of input length \(L\) has \(2^{\Omega(L)}\) pairwise inequivalent reachable prefixes at some layer, every exact diagram respecting that ordering has width \(2^{\Omega(L)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponentially many distinct residual subproblems at one layer force exponential width in every exact diagram using that ordering.
assumptions_latex: The diagram is deterministic, exact, and respects a fixed ordering.
Node merging must preserve feasible suffixes and their objective contributions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(2^{\Omega(L)}\) residual-equivalence classes imply width \(2^{\Omega(L)}\).
review_flags: The residual-equivalence lower-bound framework requires a supporting ordered decision-diagram source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-class lower-bound principle fits the exponential-width container, but its applicability to exact weighted ordered decision diagrams requires a precise supporting source and locator.

children.title: Exponential-Size Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem families whose total node or arc volume grows exponentially despite possible layerwise variation.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential-Size Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node-count lower bounds from layered residual distinctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an exact layered decision diagram, let \(w_i\) denote the number of nodes at layer \(i\). Its node count is \(|V|=\sum_{i=0}^{n}w_i\). Hence any instance family with \(w_i=2^{\Omega(L)}\) at even one layer has \(|V|=2^{\Omega(L)}\). More generally, if the sum of the numbers of pairwise inequivalent reachable residual subproblems across layers is exponential in binary input length \(L\), then every exact diagram preserving those distinctions has exponential node count, even when no single structural description explicitly enumerates all paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exponential-width layer, or exponentially many required residual states across layers, forces exponential total diagram size.
assumptions_latex: The representation is an exact layered decision diagram.
Distinct required residual subproblems cannot share a node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=0}^{n}w_i=2^{\Omega(L)}\) implies exponential diagram size.

notation.meaning: number of nodes in layer i

review_flags: No supplied source specifically supports exact decision-diagram size lower bounds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The layered node-count implication is correct and the complexity-bound kind fits, but no source supports the residual-subproblem lower-bound formulation for exact decision diagrams.

children.title: Width-to-Size Amplification
children.top_down_role: Interactions among layer count, width profiles, transition density, and total representation size.

knowledge_statements.title: Width-to-Size Amplification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates maximum layer width to total layered-diagram size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a nonempty layered decision diagram have layers \(V_0,\ldots,V_n\), widths \(w_i=|V_i|\), and maximum width \(W=\max_i w_i\). Then \(W\le |V|=\sum_{i=0}^{n}w_i\le(n+1)W\). If each node has at most \(d\) outgoing arcs, then \(|A|\le ndW\). Consequently, exponential width forces exponential node count, while polynomial width yields polynomial size whenever the number of layers and branching bound are polynomial. Conversely, small maximum width can still be amplified by a superpolynomial number of layers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total size lies between maximum width and layers times width; many layers amplify even modest width.
assumptions_latex: The diagram has \(n+1\) nonempty layers.
Every node has at most \(d\) outgoing arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W\le |V|\le(n+1)W\) and \(|A|\le ndW\).
review_flags: The counting relations are elementary, but a decision-diagram source was not supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counting inequalities are correct for the stated layered diagram, but the final superpolynomial amplification claim should explicitly identify input length as the asymptotic parameter. No inspectable decision-diagram source is supplied.

assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) is represented by a layered exact decision diagram under an ordering \(\pi\).
Each node has at most a constant number of outgoing arcs, and node equivalence can be computed in polynomial time.
\(k\) is a structural parameter of the represented instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|V(D_\pi)|=O(nf(k)n^c)\), and compilation is fixed-parameter tractable when its remaining work is polynomial per generated node.

notation.meaning: Maximum number of nodes in any layer of the diagram under ordering pi

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional parameterized bound for exact layered diagrams with bounded branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_\pi\) be an exact layered decision diagram for \(F\), with \(n+1\) node layers and maximum layer width \(W_\pi\). If a structural parameter \(k\) guarantees \(W_\pi\leq f(k)n^c\), where \(c\) is independent of \(k\), then bounded out-degree gives \[|V(D_\pi)|\leq (n+1)W_\pi=O(f(k)n^{c+1})\] and \(|A(D_\pi)|=O(|V(D_\pi)|)\). Consequently, any compiler performing polynomial work per generated node runs in \(f(k)n^{O(1)}\) time and space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a structural parameter bounds every diagram layer by an FPT expression, bounded-branching compilation has FPT size, time, and space.
knowledge_statements.title: Structural-Parameter Width Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional counting argument is plausible and the complexity_bound role fits the leaf, but no source is supplied for the decision-diagram compilation model or the claimed FPT time-and-space consequence. Source support is required before the hypotheses and compiler-cost conclusion can be relied upon.

children.title: Variable-Ordering Complexity Effect
children.top_down_role: Order-dependent representation size, bound quality, ordering-search difficulty, and adaptive-ordering overhead.

children.title: Ordering Sensitivity of Width
children.top_down_role: Variation in peak or layerwise width across variable, item, vertex, or decision orders.

assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) is fixed.
For every variable ordering, the reduced exact layered decision diagram is uniquely determined by the stated reduction convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordering sensitivity is measured by \(\max_\pi W_\pi/\min_\pi W_\pi\), which equals one exactly when all orderings have the same maximum width.

notation.meaning: Reduced exact diagram for ordering pi
Maximum layer width of the diagram

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Width comparison uses one fixed reduction convention across all variable orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each ordering \(\pi\in S_n\), let \(W_\pi=\max_{0\leq i\leq n}|L_i(D_\pi)|\). Define the width sensitivity of \(F\) by \[\operatorname{sens}_W(F)=\frac{\max_{\pi\in S_n}W_\pi}{\min_{\pi\in S_n}W_\pi}.\] This quantity is at least \(1\), equals \(1\) precisely when maximum width is invariant under ordering, and exceeds \(1\) precisely when some two orderings produce different maximum widths. The definition compares orderings of the same feasible set and does not conflate ordering effects with changes in reduction rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Width sensitivity is the ratio between the largest and smallest maximum layer widths over all variable orderings.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordering Sensitivity of Width

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ratio is internally well defined, but the record introduces it as a new definition while labeling it as a property. No source establishes this width-sensitivity measure or its intended use in the exact leaf context; an authoritative ordering-width source is needed before deciding whether the content kind should be definition or property.

children.title: Ordering Sensitivity of Diagram Size
children.top_down_role: Variation in total node and arc counts across alternative compilation orders.

assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) is fixed.
All orderings use the same exactness and reduction conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordering sensitivity is \(\max_\pi S_\pi/\min_\pi S_\pi\), with value one exactly when reduced diagram size is order-invariant.

notation.meaning: Reduced exact diagram for ordering pi
Number of nonterminal and terminal nodes in the diagram

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node-count sensitivity for reduced exact diagrams of one fixed feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each ordering \(\pi\in S_n\), let \(S_\pi=|V(D_\pi)|\). Define the diagram-size sensitivity of \(F\) by \[\operatorname{sens}_S(F)=\frac{\max_{\pi\in S_n}S_\pi}{\min_{\pi\in S_n}S_\pi}.\] It satisfies \(\operatorname{sens}_S(F)\geq1\). Equality holds exactly when every ordering yields the same reduced node count; strict inequality records ordering-induced growth. Arc-count sensitivity is equivalent up to constant factors when the decision domain, and hence maximum out-degree, is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagram-size sensitivity compares the largest and smallest reduced node counts obtainable by reordering the same variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordering Sensitivity of Diagram Size

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The node-count ratio is coherent, but it is principally a definition rather than a property. The additional arc-count equivalence requires explicit connectivity and counting conventions and is not supported by a citation. A source covering ordering-dependent reduced diagram size is required.

children.title: Width–Size Divergence by Order
children.top_down_role: Orders for which peak width and total representation size rank differently or expose different bottlenecks.

assumptions_latex: Every diagram has exactly \(n+1\) node layers.
Width and size count nodes under one common convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every ordering, \(W_\pi\leq S_\pi\leq(n+1)W_\pi\); thus width and size can rank orders differently despite this per-order coupling.

notation.meaning: Maximum layer width under ordering pi
Total node count under ordering pi

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite layered diagrams; divergence means different ordering rankings, not asymptotic independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each ordering \(\pi\), total size and maximum width obey \[S_\pi=\sum_{i=0}^{n}|L_i(D_\pi)|,\qquad W_\pi\leq S_\pi\leq(n+1)W_\pi.\] Nevertheless, for two orderings \(\pi\) and \(\sigma\), the implication \(W_\pi<W_\sigma\Rightarrow S_\pi<S_\sigma\) need not hold: one diagram may have a narrow peak but many moderately wide layers, while another has a wider peak concentrated in fewer layers. Thus minimizing maximum width and minimizing total size are distinct ordering objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Size is the sum of layer widths, so orders minimizing peak width need not minimize total nodes, although both measures differ by at most the layer count.
knowledge_statements.title: Width–Size Divergence by Order

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The per-order inequalities follow from the stated layer-count convention, but the existential claim that width and size can rank two orders differently is the substantive divergence claim and has neither a cited source nor an inspectable example. Source support is required for that claim and its decision-diagram context.

assumptions_latex: Each ordering produces a relaxed diagram whose accepted language contains the exact feasible set.
The objective value of a path is evaluated consistently across diagrams.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Language inclusion implies bound dominance; without inclusion, bounds from two orderings have no general dominance relation.

notation.meaning: Relaxed language produced under ordering pi and width limit B
Maximization upper bound from the relaxed diagram

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization bounds from width-limited relaxed diagrams; reverse inequalities apply to minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximization problem with feasible set \(F\), let \(F\subseteq R_{\pi,B}\) be the language of a width-limited relaxed diagram and define \(U_{\pi,B}=\max\{c(x):x\in R_{\pi,B}\}\). Then \(U_{\pi,B}\) is a valid upper bound. If \(R_{\pi,B}\subseteq R_{\sigma,B}\), then \(U_{\pi,B}\leq U_{\sigma,B}\). When neither relaxed language contains the other, validity alone yields no ordering-independent comparison between \(U_{\pi,B}\) and \(U_{\sigma,B}\); either ordering may provide the tighter bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A narrower relaxed language gives a tighter maximization bound, but orderings producing incomparable relaxations can yield bounds in either order.
knowledge_statements.title: Order-Dependent Bound Quality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The language-inclusion bound comparison is mathematically coherent for maximization and the property role fits the leaf. However, no source is supplied for the width-limited relaxed-diagram semantics or for the order-dependent incomparability claim, so the record cannot yet be accepted as candidate-review knowledge.

assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) distinct decision variables.
A fixed-order compiler and objective evaluator terminate for every ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exhaustive ordering search costs \(O(n!T_{\max})\) time and \(O(M_{\max})\) reusable working space.

notation.meaning: Compilation and evaluation time for ordering pi
Maximum reusable working memory for one ordering

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case enumeration bound; it does not assert hardness of a particular ordering objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To find an ordering minimizing any exactly computable diagram score \(q(\pi)\), exhaustive search compiles and evaluates every \(\pi\in S_n\), retaining an incumbent of smallest score. Its running time is \[\sum_{\pi\in S_n}T(\pi)=O(n!T_{\max}),\qquad T_{\max}=\max_{\pi\in S_n}T(\pi).\] If diagrams are discarded after evaluation, working space is \(O(M_{\max})\), apart from storage for the incumbent. The factorial factor counts candidate permutations and is independent of the internal compiler complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact brute-force ordering search evaluates all factorially many variable permutations and can reuse the memory needed for one compilation.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordering-Search Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The factorial enumeration accounting is plausible and the complexity_bound role fits. No evidence is supplied for the decision-diagram ordering-search setting, and the reusable-space statement depends on what must be retained as the incumbent. A source specifying that computational model is required.

assumptions_latex: An adaptive compiler may revise the unprocessed variable suffix at finitely many decision points.
Each revision preserves the semantics required by the chosen exact or relaxed diagram type.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Total adaptive overhead is bounded by the sum of ordering-decision, invalidation, and rebuilding costs over all revisions.

notation.meaning: Invalidation and rebuilding cost at revision j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accounting bound for online reordering during diagram compilation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a baseline fixed-order compilation costs \(T_{\mathrm{base}}\). If an adaptive procedure makes \(r\) ordering revisions, where revision \(j\) spends \(H_j\) selecting a new suffix and \(R_j\) invalidating or rebuilding affected states and arcs, then its total time satisfies \[T_{\mathrm{adaptive}}\leq T_{\mathrm{base}}+\sum_{j=1}^{r}(H_j+R_j).\] Hence the additive adaptive-ordering overhead is at most \(\sum_{j=1}^{r}(H_j+R_j)\). Any claimed improvement must be compared against this overhead and the compilation work actually avoided.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive reordering adds the costs of choosing new orders and rebuilding invalidated diagram portions; savings must exceed this accumulated overhead.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Ordering Overhead

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated assumptions do not ensure that ordinary adaptive compilation work is bounded by the fixed-order baseline. Changing the suffix can alter the number and cost of generated states independently of the listed selection and rebuilding charges. A source or a more explicit accounting model is needed to determine valid hypotheses and the correct bound.

children.title: Knapsack Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision diagrams for single-resource or multidimensional knapsack structure, capacity states, and item choices.

assumptions_latex: \(a_i\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\), and \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\).
Variables are processed in a fixed ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Root-to-terminal paths are in bijection with vectors satisfying \(\sum_i a_ix_i\leq b\).

notation.meaning: Cumulative used capacity after a prefix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact capacity-state diagram for a binary single-constraint knapsack set.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the knapsack set \(K=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n a_ix_i\leq b\}\), construct layer \(i\) from reachable cumulative weights after the first \(i\) decisions. From state \(s\), an arc labeled \(x_i=0\) goes to \(s\), and an arc labeled \(x_i=1\) goes to \(s+a_i\) exactly when \(s+a_i\leq b\). The root state is \(0\); every state after layer \(n\) is accepting. The resulting diagram represents exactly \(K\) and has width at most \(b+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary knapsack diagram tracks used capacity; taking an item adds its weight when capacity remains, and every surviving final state is feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Knapsack Diagrams

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The capacity-state representation is precise and the representation role fits the leaf, but the cited locator concerns knapsack cuts and is flagged as supporting only the underlying knapsack model. It does not establish the decision-diagram construction, exact path correspondence, or width bound. A specific decision-diagram or dynamic-programming encoding source is required.

children.title: Resource-Allocation Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision diagrams for assigning limited resources across activities, agents, projects, or time periods.

assumptions_latex: Each decision domain \(X_i\) is finite.
Resource consumptions \(a_i(x_i)\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}^m\) and capacity \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}^m\) are componentwise nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted paths represent exactly the allocations satisfying \(\sum_i a_i(x_i)\leq b\).

notation.meaning: Finite allocation choices for activity i
Resource-consumption vector of choice x at activity i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact cumulative-resource diagram for finite multidimensional allocation choices.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 Resource allocation in production planning p. 4

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(X=\{x\in\prod_{i=1}^nX_i:\sum_{i=1}^na_i(x_i)\leq b\}\), with componentwise inequality. A layered diagram starts at \(s=0\). At layer \(i\), state \(s\) has an arc labeled \(x_i\in X_i\) to \(s'=s+a_i(x_i)\) exactly when \(s'\leq b\). All states in the final layer are accepting. Every root-to-terminal path therefore specifies one feasible allocation, and every feasible allocation induces one such path. The width is bounded by \(\prod_{j=1}^m(b_j+1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resource-allocation diagram tracks cumulative use of each capacity and admits a choice exactly when the updated resource vector remains feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Allocation Diagrams

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.1 Resource allocation in production planning p. 4

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cumulative-resource construction is mathematically plausible and appropriately classified as a representation. The cited resource-allocation section supports the model but not the diagram encoding, exact path correspondence, or product width bound. A source with a specific locator for the state-space representation is required.

children.title: Shared Resource-State Encodings
children.top_down_role: State organizations shared across knapsack and allocation settings, including residual-capacity and usage-profile views.

assumptions_latex: Future resource feasibility depends on a prefix only through its cumulative resource vector.
All resource contributions are additive across decisions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Merging equal-resource prefix states preserves the represented feasible suffixes and therefore preserves exactness.

notation.meaning: Cumulative resource vector of prefix p
Set of feasible suffix decisions following prefix p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient state-merging rule for additive capacity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a prefix \(p=(x_1,\ldots,x_i)\), define \(s(p)=\sum_{j=1}^ia_j(x_j)\). If two prefixes \(p\) and \(q\) lie in the same layer and satisfy \(s(p)=s(q)\), then for every suffix \(y\), \[s(p)+\sum_{j=i+1}^na_j(y_j)\leq b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad s(q)+\sum_{j=i+1}^na_j(y_j)\leq b.\] Hence \(C(p)=C(q)\), so the prefixes may share one diagram node without changing the accepted feasible set. Equal resource state is sufficient, though not necessarily necessary, for exact merging.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prefixes with the same cumulative resource use admit exactly the same capacity-feasible suffixes and can share a decision-diagram state.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared Resource-State Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equal-resource-state merging rule matches the leaf and is stated consistently, but no source supports the decision-diagram equivalence criterion or its exactness consequence. The broad assumptions also need to be tied to a precisely sourced additive-capacity model.

children.title: Packing Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision diagrams for conflict-limited selection, capacity packing, and mutually compatible subsets.

assumptions_latex: Variables are processed in a fixed ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted paths are exactly the set-packing vectors satisfying \(Ax\leq\mathbf1\).

notation.meaning: Incidence matrix of elements versus selectable sets
Binary vector of already occupied rows
Incidence column of selectable set i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact occupied-row encoding for binary set packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax\leq\mathbf1\}\), let a state \(s\in\{0,1\}^m\) record rows already occupied by selected columns. From \(s\), the arc labeled \(x_i=0\) retains \(s\). The arc labeled \(x_i=1\) exists exactly when \(s+A_{\cdot i}\leq\mathbf1\), and then reaches \(s+A_{\cdot i}\). The root is \(0\), and every final state accepts. Thus paths and feasible packings correspond exactly; equivalent reachable states may be merged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-packing diagram records occupied elements and allows selecting a set only when it does not overlap any previously selected set.
knowledge_statements.title: Packing Diagrams

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The occupied-row construction is a coherent exact representation of binary set packing, and representation is the correct content kind. The cited section supports the packing formulation but not the decision-diagram state construction, path correspondence, or merging statement. A diagram-specific or state-space source is required.

children.title: Covering Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision diagrams for requirement coverage, residual-demand states, and coverage redundancy.

assumptions_latex: Variables are processed in a fixed ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepting paths are exactly the set-covering vectors satisfying \(Ax\geq\mathbf1\).

notation.meaning: Incidence matrix of elements versus selectable sets
Binary vector of rows already covered

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact capped-coverage encoding for binary set covering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax\geq\mathbf1\}\), let state \(s\in\{0,1\}^m\) indicate rows already covered. From \(s\), an arc labeled \(x_i=0\) retains \(s\), while an arc labeled \(x_i=1\) reaches \(s'=\mathbf1\wedge(s+A_{\cdot i})\), where the minimum is componentwise. The root is \(0\), and only final state \(\mathbf1\) accepts. Thus a path accepts exactly when its selected columns cover every row; identical coverage states may be merged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-covering diagram tracks which elements are covered, caps coverage at one, and accepts only paths covering every element.
knowledge_statements.title: Covering Diagrams

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The capped-coverage construction is coherent and the representation role fits the leaf. The cited packing-and-covering section supports the set-covering formulation but does not support the decision-diagram encoding, accepting-state rule, or state-merging claim. A source with a specific locator for this representation is required.

children.title: Partitioning Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision diagrams for exact assignment or exact coverage structures with exclusivity requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Partitioning Diagrams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact binary decision-diagram representation of set partitioning solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be finite and let \(\mathcal S=(S_1,\ldots,S_m)\) be subsets of \(U\). A partitioning diagram for this ordered family is a layered acyclic binary diagram whose source-to-terminal paths have arc labels \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\{0,1\}\) and satisfy
\[
\mathcal P=\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^m:\sum_{i:u\in S_i}x_i=1\text{ for every }u\in U\right\}.
\]
The diagram is exact when the path-label map is a bijection between its source-to-terminal paths and \(\mathcal P\). Thus each path selects a subfamily that contains every element of \(U\) exactly once.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact partitioning diagram has one path per subfamily that covers every ground-set element exactly once.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(\mathcal S\) are finite.
The variables are processed in the fixed order \(1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The source-to-terminal path labels are exactly the incidence vectors in \(\mathcal P\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact-cover path representation is mathematically unambiguous

knowledge_statements.title: Conflict-Graph Selection Diagrams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact diagram representation of selections subject to pairwise conflicts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) with ordered vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\), a conflict-graph selection diagram is a layered binary decision diagram whose decision at layer \(i\) is whether to select \(v_i\). It is exact when its source-to-terminal path labels are precisely
\[
\mathcal I(G)=\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^{V}:x_u+x_v\le 1\text{ for every }\{u,v\}\in E\right\}.
\]
Consequently, every accepted path encodes a conflict-free selection, and every conflict-free selection has exactly one accepted path under the fixed variable order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accepted paths correspond bijectively to vertex selections containing no adjacent pair in the conflict graph.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple graph.
A fixed ordering of \(V\) determines the diagram layers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted path vectors equal \(\mathcal I(G)\), the stable-set incidence vectors of \(G\).

source_refs.locator: 2.4.1 Set Packing and Stable Sets p. 51

children.title: Permutation Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision diagrams for complete orderings, remaining-element states, position choices, and permutation restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Permutation Diagrams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Layered diagram whose paths encode all permutations of a finite set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite set with \(|V|=n\). The canonical permutation diagram has layer \(k\) states indexed by subsets \(S\subseteq V\) with \(|S|=k\), a source state \(\varnothing\), and, for every \(v\in V\setminus S\), an arc labeled \(v\) from \(S\) to \(S\cup\{v\}\). Its unique terminal state is \(V\). Every source-to-terminal path therefore has a label sequence \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) in which each member of \(V\) occurs exactly once, and every permutation of \(V\) determines exactly one such path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subset states and unused-element transitions give a bijection between terminal paths and permutations of the ground set.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite with \(|V|=n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Source-to-terminal label sequences are in bijection with the permutations of \(V\).

notation.meaning: elements already placed in the partial permutation

children.title: Sequence Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision diagrams for partial or variable-length sequences, contextual states, and admissible continuations.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequence Diagrams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite acyclic diagrams representing constrained finite-word languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Sigma\) be a finite alphabet and let \(L\subseteq\bigcup_{k=0}^{n}\Sigma^k\). A sequence diagram for \(L\) is a finite rooted acyclic directed graph with arcs labeled in \(\Sigma\), designated accepting vertices, and path length at most \(n\), such that the concatenated labels of root-to-accepting paths are exactly the words in \(L\). It is deterministic when each vertex has at most one outgoing arc bearing any given label. It is exact and unambiguous when every word in \(L\) labels exactly one root-to-accepting path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence diagram is an acyclic labeled graph whose accepting paths encode exactly a specified finite language of bounded-length sequences.
assumptions_latex: \(\Sigma\) is finite.
\(L\subseteq\bigcup_{k=0}^{n}\Sigma^k\) for some finite \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepting path language of the diagram is exactly \(L\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise, internally consistent, and appropriate for the Sequence Diagrams leaf, but no inspectable citation supports this use of the term or its exact path-language semantics.

children.title: Permutation-to-Sequence Generalizations
children.top_down_role: Changes in state structure when complete permutations are relaxed to optional, repeated, or truncated sequences.

knowledge_statements.title: Permutation-to-Sequence Generalizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutations arise as a cardinality-constrained special case of sequence languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite alphabet \(V\) and multiplicity bounds \(b_v\in\mathbb Z_+\), define
\[
L_b=\left\{(v_1,\ldots,v_k):0\le k\le\sum_{v\in V}b_v,\;\#\{i:v_i=v\}\le b_v\text{ for every }v\in V\right\}.
\]
A sequence diagram for \(L_b\) may use the count vector \(c\) as state and append \(v\) precisely when \(c_v<b_v\). When \(b_v=1\) for every \(v\in V\) and acceptance requires length \(|V|\), the accepted language is exactly the permutation language. Allowing larger bounds, optional termination, or restricted transitions produces repeated-element and constrained-sequence generalizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Permutation diagrams are sequence diagrams with unit symbol capacities and full-length acceptance; larger capacities or transition restrictions yield broader sequence models.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(b\in\mathbb Z_+^V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unit bounds and length \(|V|\) recover permutations; general bounds define bounded-multiplicity sequences.

notation.meaning: vector of multiplicities used so far

children.title: Single-Machine Scheduling Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision diagrams for job selection, machine availability, timing context, and single-resource schedules.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Machine Scheduling Diagrams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact earliest-start state diagram for nonpreemptive single-machine schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J\) be a finite job set with processing times \(p_j>0\), release dates \(r_j\ge 0\), and deadlines \(d_j\ge r_j+p_j\). A scheduling-diagram state \((S,t)\) records completed jobs and the completion time of their earliest-start partial schedule. From \((S,t)\), choosing \(j\notin S\) gives
\[
t'=\max\{t,r_j\}+p_j,
\]
and creates an arc to \((S\cup\{j\},t')\) exactly when \(t'\le d_j\). The source is \((\varnothing,0)\), and states with \(S=J\) are terminal. Terminal paths correspond exactly to job orders whose earliest-start nonpreemptive schedules satisfy every release date and deadline.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: States track completed jobs and completion time; feasible arcs append jobs at their earliest possible start, yielding exactly the deadline-feasible earliest-start schedules.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite and every job must be processed once.
\(p_j\in\mathbb R_{>0}\), \(r_j\in\mathbb R_+\), and \(d_j\in\mathbb R\) with \(d_j\ge r_j+p_j\) for every \(j\in J\).
The machine processes at most one job at a time without preemption.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Terminal paths encode exactly the feasible job orders under earliest-start scheduling.

notation.meaning: completion time of the earliest-start partial schedule represented by the path
release date, processing time, and deadline of job j

children.title: Sequencing-State Encodings
children.top_down_role: State representations for completed jobs, predecessor context, accumulated time, and sequence-dependent attributes.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequencing-State Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness criterion for merging partial sequences into diagram states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h\) and \(h'\) be feasible partial sequences. A state encoding \(\phi\) is exact only if
\[
\phi(h)=\phi(h')\Longrightarrow \mathcal C(h)=\mathcal C(h')
\]
and, for every common continuation \(z\in\mathcal C(h)\), the incremental objective values satisfy \(\Delta(h,z)=\Delta(h',z)\). Here \(\mathcal C(h)\) is the set of feasible continuations after \(h\). Under this condition, merging histories with equal encoded states preserves both the feasible complete sequences and their path costs. Typical components include the used-job set, current time, last job, and accumulated resources, but only components needed to satisfy the implication are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two partial sequences may share a state only when they admit identical continuations with identical incremental costs.
assumptions_latex: The sequencing problem has a well-defined feasible-continuation set and additive path costs.
\(h\) and \(h'\) end at the same diagram layer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Merging equal encoded states preserves feasibility and objective values when the displayed continuation condition holds.

notation.meaning: incremental cost of continuation z after h

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-continuation condition fits a state-encoding condition leaf, but the necessity and cost-preservation formulation depend on the precise diagram and path-cost model. No source is supplied to establish that version.

children.title: Timing-Resource Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits introduced by time windows, setup effects, release conditions, and high-dimensional temporal state.

knowledge_statements.title: Timing-Resource Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A used-job set alone fails when timing depends on sequence history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider jobs \(a,b,c\) with unit processing times, zero initial setup times, and sequence-dependent setups \(s_{ab}=0\), \(s_{ba}=2\), \(s_{ac}=s_{bc}=0\). Let only job \(c\) have the binding deadline \(d_c=3\). After completing \(S=\{a,b\}\), order \((a,b)\) finishes at time \(2\), whereas order \((b,a)\) finishes at time \(4\). Appending \(c\) to the first history completes it at time \(3\) and is feasible; appending it to the second completes it at time \(5\) and is infeasible. Hence \(S\) alone is not an exact state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequence-dependent timing can give two histories with the same completed-job set different feasible continuations, so a subset-only state is invalid.
assumptions_latex: Jobs are processed nonpreemptively on one machine.
Setup time is incurred between consecutive jobs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any exact encoding for this instance must distinguish the two histories, for example by time or sequence information.

notation.meaning: setup time when job j follows job i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The calculations are internally correct and demonstrate the stated subset-state failure, and failure_boundary is the appropriate kind. The constructed counterexample nevertheless has no cited or registered evidence.

children.title: Routing Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision diagrams for path construction, vehicle movement, resource tracking, and route feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Routing Diagrams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subset-state representation of elementary directed source-to-sink routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with distinct vertices \(s,t\). An elementary-routing diagram has states \((v,S)\), where \(v\in S\subseteq V\), \(s\in S\), and \(S\) is the set of visited vertices. Its source is \((s,\{s\})\). For each \((v,w)\in A\) with \(w\notin S\), it has an arc labeled \((v,w)\) from \((v,S)\) to \((w,S\cup\{w\})\); states whose current vertex is \(t\) are terminal and have no outgoing arcs. Terminal paths are therefore in bijection with elementary directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) routes in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tracking the current and visited vertices yields one terminal path for every elementary directed source-to-sink route.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
\(s,t\in V\) are distinct.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Terminal diagram paths correspond bijectively to elementary directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) routes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The visited-set construction is precise and yields the claimed bijection for elementary directed routes, but no inspectable diagram-specific source is provided.

children.title: Tour Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision diagrams for closed visits, customer coverage, return requirements, and tour-specific state.

knowledge_statements.title: Tour Diagrams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subset-and-endpoint diagram for directed Hamiltonian tours.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with depot \(0\in V\). A tour diagram has source \((\{0\},0)\) and states \((S,v)\), where \(0,v\in S\subseteq V\) and \(v\) is the last visited vertex. It contains a transition from \((S,v)\) to \((S\cup\{w\},w)\) when \(w\notin S\) and \((v,w)\in A\). From every state \((V,v)\) with \((v,0)\in A\), a terminal arc returns to \(0\). Source-to-terminal paths are in bijection with directed Hamiltonian tours based at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Visited-set and last-vertex states encode exactly the depot-based directed Hamiltonian tours.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and directed.
The depot \(0\in V\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each terminal path visits every vertex exactly once before returning to \(0\), and every such tour has one path.

children.title: Resource-Constrained Route States
children.top_down_role: State tracking for capacity, time, visited sets, location, and route-dependent resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Constrained Route States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact route states augment location and history with accumulated resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each arc \(e\in A\) consume a nonnegative vector \(d_e\in\mathbb R_+^q\), and let \(Q\in\mathbb R_+^q\) be the resource limit. A resource-constrained elementary-route state is \((v,S,r)\), where \(v\) is the current vertex, \(S\) is the visited set, and \(r\) is cumulative consumption. Traversing \(e=(v,w)\) with \(w\notin S\) is allowed exactly when \(r+d_e\le Q\) componentwise and produces \((w,S\cup\{w\},r+d_e)\). Starting from \((s,\{s\},0)\), terminal paths at \(t\) encode exactly the elementary \(s\)-to-\(t\) routes satisfying all resource limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A route state tracks endpoint, visited vertices, and resource consumption; feasible transitions yield exactly the resource-bounded elementary routes.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
\(d_e\in\mathbb R_+^q\) for every \(e\in A\).
Resource feasibility means componentwise consumption at most \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Terminal paths are exactly the elementary routes whose total resource vector does not exceed \(Q\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive resource-state update is mathematically precise, agrees with the plain statement, and fits a representation leaf. No inspectable resource-constrained routing source is supplied.

children.title: Stable-Set Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision diagrams for selecting mutually nonadjacent vertices under vertex-order or frontier-state compilation.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set Diagrams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact frontier-state diagram for stable sets under a vertex ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have vertex order \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\). At cut \(i\), let \(F_i\) contain processed vertices adjacent to an unprocessed vertex. A frontier state records \(B\subseteq F_i\), the selected frontier vertices. At layer \(i+1\), exclusion of \(v_{i+1}\) is always allowed; inclusion is allowed exactly when \(B\cap N(v_{i+1})=\varnothing\). After either decision, vertices leaving the frontier are deleted from \(B\), and an included \(v_{i+1}\) is retained when it belongs to the new frontier. The resulting source-to-terminal paths are in bijection with the stable sets of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Frontier states retain selected boundary vertices, allowing exactly those inclusion decisions that preserve stability.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple graph.
A fixed vertex order defines the successive frontiers \(F_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The diagram accepts exactly the incidence vectors of stable sets of \(G\).

notation.meaning: selected vertices currently on the frontier

children.title: Clique Diagrams

knowledge_statements.title: Clique Diagrams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact layered decision diagrams for clique incidence vectors under a fixed vertex ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph with ordering \(V=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\). A clique diagram is a layered acyclic decision diagram whose layer-\(i\) arcs are labeled by \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\), and whose root-to-accepting-terminal label sequences are exactly
\[\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^n: x_i+x_j\le 1\ \text{for every }\{v_i,v_j\}\notin E\right\}.\]
Thus each accepting path represents the clique \(C(x)=\{v_i:x_i=1\}\); assigning arc cost \(w_i x_i\) makes a longest root-to-terminal path represent a maximum-weight clique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The diagram accepts exactly the binary incidence vectors of cliques; weighted longest-path optimization therefore solves maximum-weight clique.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, simple, and vertex ordered.
\(w\in\mathbb{R}^V\) when weighted optimization is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is accepted}\iff C(x)\text{ is a clique of }G\).

notation.meaning: indicator that vertex v_i belongs to the clique

children.title: Complement-Graph Transfer
children.top_down_role: Representation correspondence, ordering effects, and complexity changes when transferring between complementary graph views.

knowledge_statements.title: Complement-Graph Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer between stable-set and clique diagrams using graph complementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(\overline G\) have vertex set \(V\) and edges \(\{u,v\}\) precisely when \(u\ne v\) and \(\{u,v\}\notin E\). Then, for every \(S\subseteq V\),
\[S\text{ is a clique of }G\iff S\text{ is a stable set of }\overline G.\]
Consequently, under the same vertex ordering, any exact stable-set decision diagram for \(\overline G\) is an exact clique decision diagram for \(G\) after preserving every binary arc label and vertex weight; the represented incidence vectors and path objective values are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cliques of a graph are stable sets of its complement, so an exact stable-set diagram transfers unchanged to an exact clique diagram.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph.
The two diagrams use the same vertex ordering and binary labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C(G)=\mathcal S(\overline G)\), with identical diagram paths and weights.

notation.meaning: family of stable sets of G

children.title: Cut Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision diagrams for vertex-side assignments, edge contributions, connectivity context, and cut objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Diagrams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frontier-state representation of weighted vertex bipartitions and their cut values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph with vertex ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) and edge weights \(w_e\). A cut diagram branches on side labels \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\). At layer \(i\), its state records the labels of processed vertices incident to unprocessed vertices. When an edge \(e=\{v_j,v_i\}\) becomes fully processed, its contribution \(w_e|x_j-x_i|\) is added exactly once and may then be forgotten. Every complete path represents one bipartition, and its accumulated value is
\[W(x)=\sum_{\{v_i,v_j\}\in E}w_{ij}|x_i-x_j|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut diagram stores side assignments only on the active frontier and accumulates each crossing-edge weight when that edge becomes fully processed.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and vertex ordered.
\(w_e\in\mathbb{R}\) for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{path-value}(x)=W(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^V\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: frontier dynamic programming charges an edge when its second endpoint is processed

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The frontier construction and edge-charging rule are coherent and correctly reproduce the cut value, but no inspectable source supports this specialized decision-diagram representation.

children.title: Coloring Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision diagrams for color assignments, conflict tracking, available-color profiles, and symmetry effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring Diagrams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact frontier-state diagrams for proper colorings with a fixed color bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph with ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), and fix \(q\ge1\). A coloring diagram has layer-\(i\) arcs labeled by \(c_i\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\). A transition is retained exactly when \(c_i\ne c_j\) for every already processed neighbor \(v_j\) of \(v_i\). The state after layer \(i\) retains the colors only of processed vertices adjacent to an unprocessed vertex. Its accepting paths are therefore exactly
\[\left\{c\in\{1,\ldots,q\}^{V}:c_u\ne c_v\ \text{for every }\{u,v\}\in E\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The diagram assigns colors sequentially, retains colors on the active frontier, and accepts exactly the proper colorings using at most q colors.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and vertex ordered.
\(q\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\text{ is accepted}\iff c\text{ is a proper }q\text{-coloring of }G\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: all future coloring constraints depend only on colors of frontier vertices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly characterizes an exact frontier diagram for fixed-q proper coloring, but the specialized representation has no cited source.

children.title: Shared Frontier Encodings
children.top_down_role: Frontier-state structures usable across cut and coloring formulations under graph orderings.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared Frontier Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified boundary signatures for cut and coloring decision diagrams.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), define the frontier after layer \(i\) by
\[F_i=\{v_j:j\le i,\ \exists \ell>i\text{ with }\{v_j,v_\ell\}\in E\}.\]
A shared frontier encoding maps a partial assignment to its restriction on \(F_i\), together with any accumulated objective value kept on arcs. For cuts, the restriction lies in \(\{0,1\}^{F_i}\); for \(q\)-coloring, it lies in \(\{1,\ldots,q\}^{F_i}\). Two partial assignments with the same restriction have identical feasible continuations and identical future incremental contributions, so their diagram nodes may be merged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut and coloring diagrams use the same active frontier, differing only in the labels stored at frontier vertices.
assumptions_latex: Future constraints are graph edges between processed and unprocessed vertices.
Completed-edge objective contributions are charged before their endpoints are forgotten.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_i(a)=\sigma_i(b)\Rightarrow\) partial assignments \(a,b\) have the same continuation subproblem.

notation.meaning: processed vertices adjacent to unprocessed vertices

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equal boundary assignments induce equal residual edge subproblems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shared frontier signature is plausible for the stated cut and coloring models, but the residual-equivalence and node-merging claim needs an inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.title: Frontier-Based Graph Diagrams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Layered graph decision diagrams whose states summarize the active vertex boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\) and ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), the frontier at layer \(i\) is
\[F_i=\{v_j:j\le i,\ \exists \ell>i\text{ such that }\{v_j,v_\ell\}\in E\}.\]
A frontier-based graph diagram is a layered decision diagram processing \(v_i\) at layer \(i\), whose state is a sufficient signature on \(F_i\): whenever two partial assignments share the signature, they admit the same feasible completions and the same future objective contribution. Vertices outside \(F_i\) are forgotten because no unprocessed edge is incident to them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A frontier-based diagram stores precisely a sufficient summary of processed vertices that still interact by edges with unprocessed vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and simple.
A fixed vertex ordering is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_i(a)=s_i(b)\Rightarrow\mathcal R_i(a)=\mathcal R_i(b)\), where \(\mathcal R_i\) is the residual subproblem.

notation.meaning: active frontier after processing layer i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: frontier signatures are residual-subproblem equivalence classes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the topic and is internally consistent, but no authoritative source is supplied for the frontier-state sufficiency formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Resource-State Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Width bound for diagrams tracking finitely bounded additive resource totals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a layered decision diagram tracks an integer resource vector \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_d)\), initialized at zero and updated additively by each decision. If every reachable state satisfies \(0\le r_j\le B_j\) and feasibility and future costs depend on the history only through \(r\), then states having the same vector may be merged. Hence every layer has at most
\[\prod_{j=1}^{d}(B_j+1)\]
resource states. For fixed \(d\), construction is polynomial in the numeric bounds \(B_j\), but generally only pseudopolynomial in their binary encoding lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded integer resource totals yield at most the product of their range sizes in each layer, producing a pseudopolynomial diagram bound.
assumptions_latex: \(r_j\in\{0,\ldots,B_j\}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,d\).
The resource vector is a sufficient state statistic.
Resource updates are additive and integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{width}\le\prod_{j=1}^{d}(B_j+1)\).

notation.meaning: upper bound on resource coordinate j

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 Resource allocation in production planning p. 4

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.1 Resource allocation in production planning p. 4

children.title: Bounded-Separator Regimes
children.top_down_role: Graph or decomposition structures whose intercomponent interaction is controlled by small separators.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Separator Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-label decomposition regimes with uniformly bounded interaction separators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a sequence of processed vertex sets \(P_i\subseteq V\) and their unprocessed complements \(U_i=V\setminus P_i\). A bounded-separator regime holds when there are sets \(S_i\subseteq P_i\) and a constant \(k\) such that \(|S_i|\le k\), every edge from \(P_i\) to \(U_i\) has its processed endpoint in \(S_i\), and the residual subproblem depends on decisions in \(P_i\) only through labels assigned to \(S_i\). If each separator vertex has at most \(q\) labels, at most \(q^k\) distinct separator assignments occur at any layer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regime is bounded-separator when all processed-to-unprocessed interaction passes through at most k labeled processed vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite.
Each separator vertex has at most \(q\) possible labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|S_i|\le k\) and separator sufficiency imply at most \(q^k\) separator-label states.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: bounded labeled separators bound the number of boundary assignments

children.title: Bounded Frontier-State Regimes
children.top_down_role: Compilation orders whose active boundary admits a bounded number of relevant state configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Frontier-State Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagram-width bound induced by a uniformly bounded active frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) be a graph ordering with frontiers \(F_i\). Suppose \(|F_i|\le k\) for every layer, each frontier vertex carries one of at most \(q\) local labels, and the state additionally carries one of at most \(r\) global summaries. If these data determine the residual subproblem, equal states may be merged and the exact diagram satisfies
\[\operatorname{width}_i\le r q^{|F_i|}\le r q^k\quad\text{for every }i.\]
Thus fixed \(k,q,r\) give bounded exact width and a diagram with \(O(nrq^k)\) nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A frontier of at most k vertices with q labels and r summaries yields exact width at most r times q to the k.
assumptions_latex: \(|F_i|\le k\) for all layers.
Each frontier vertex has at most \(q\) labels.
There are at most \(r\) sufficient global summaries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{width}\le rq^k\) and \(|N|=O(nrq^k)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: count all sufficient assignments on a bounded frontier

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counting bound and node bound follow from the stated sufficient-state assumptions and fit the leaf, but no source is provided for the exact-diagram width result.

children.title: Separator-to-Frontier Transfer
children.top_down_role: How separator structure influences frontier size, state requirements, and diagram compilation behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Separator-to-Frontier Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-separation formulation relating bounded separators to bounded graph frontiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite. For an ordering \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), define \(F_i\) as the processed vertices adjacent to an unprocessed vertex and set \(\operatorname{vs}(\pi)=\max_i|F_i|\). Then
\[\min_{\pi}\operatorname{vs}(\pi)=\operatorname{pw}(G),\]
where \(\operatorname{pw}(G)\) is pathwidth. In particular, an ordering with frontier size at most \(k\) yields bags \(B_i=F_{i-1}\cup\{v_i\}\) of size at most \(k+1\), hence a path decomposition of width at most \(k\); conversely, a width-\(k\) path decomposition admits an ordering with frontier size at most \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum maximum frontier size equals pathwidth, so bounded path separators and bounded frontier orderings transfer without asymptotic width loss.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
Path-decomposition width is maximum bag size minus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{\pi}\max_i|F_i|=\operatorname{pw}(G)\).

notation.meaning: path-decomposition bag induced by the ordering

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical equality between vertex separation number and pathwidth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equality between vertex separation number and pathwidth is a classical theorem, but it is convention-sensitive and requires a specific authoritative theorem or section citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Separable State Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State aggregation for block objectives coupled through low-dimensional additive summaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let variables be partitioned into blocks \(x=(x^1,\ldots,x^m)\), with objective \(\sum_{b=1}^m f_b(x^b)\) and coupling condition \(\sum_{b=1}^m A_bx^b\in K\). Processing blocks sequentially gives the state
\[s_i=\sum_{b=1}^{i}A_bx^b.\]
If feasibility of completing blocks \(i+1,\ldots,m\) and all future costs depend on earlier choices only through \(s_i\), partial solutions with equal \(s_i\) may be merged. An exact block-separable decision diagram branches over feasible block assignments, updates \(s_i=s_{i-1}+A_ix^i\), and accepts precisely when \(s_m\in K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For block-separable models, cumulative coupling contributions form an exact state whenever they completely determine feasible continuations.
assumptions_latex: \(x^b\in X_b\) for finite block domains \(X_b\).
The objective is \(\sum_b f_b(x^b)\).
Coupling is determined by \(\sum_b A_bx^b\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_i(a)=s_i(b)\Rightarrow\mathcal R_i(a)=\mathcal R_i(b)\), and acceptance is equivalent to \(s_m\in K\).

notation.meaning: cumulative coupling state through block i
admissible set for the final coupling sum

children.title: State-Space Explosion
children.top_down_role: Growth caused by adverse problem structure, insufficient compression, or high-dimensional state.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Exact Width
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit residual-state family forcing exponential width under an unfavorable ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(m\ge1\), consider binary variables \((x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_m)\), ordered with all \(x\)-variables first, and feasible set
\[L_m=\{(x,y)\in\{0,1\}^{2m}:y_i=x_i\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\}.\]
After processing \((x_1,\ldots,x_m)\), each vector \(a\in\{0,1\}^m\) has the unique feasible continuation \(y=a\). Distinct vectors therefore induce distinct residual feasible sets and cannot share a node in any exact deterministic decision diagram respecting this ordering. Consequently its middle-layer width is at least \(2^m\); the diagram storing \(a\) attains width \(2^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Processing all copied bits before their matches forces an exact diagram to remember every binary prefix, giving middle width exactly two to the m.
assumptions_latex: The diagram is deterministic and exact.
The variable order is \((x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_m)\).
Nodes may merge only when their feasible continuation sets agree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{width}_m=2^m\) for the reduced exact diagram of \(L_m\) in the stated ordering.

notation.meaning: assignment to the first m variables

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distinct residual continuation sets require distinct deterministic diagram nodes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The copy-equality family gives the stated exponential residual-state lower bound under the fixed ordering, and the complexity-bound kind fits the leaf. An inspectable source is still required for the deterministic exact-diagram lower-bound principle.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Dimension Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact layered diagrams for independent, discrete resource coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a layered decision diagram whose exact state after a prefix is the residual-resource vector \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_d)\). Suppose that, at some layer, every vector in \(R_1\times\cdots\times R_d\) is reachable and that distinct vectors have distinct feasible-continuation sets. Exact reduction cannot merge any two such states. Consequently that layer has width at least \(\prod_{j=1}^d |R_j|\). In particular, if \(|R_j|\ge 2\) for every \(j\), exact width is at least \(2^d\), so increasing the resource dimension causes exponential state-space growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent resource coordinates yield multiplicative exact width; two reachable values per coordinate already force width at least exponential in the resource dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb N\) resource coordinates are represented exactly.
Every vector in \(R_1\times\cdots\times R_d\) is reachable at one layer.
Distinct residual vectors admit distinct feasible-continuation sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{width}\ge \prod_{j=1}^{d}|R_j|,\qquad |R_j|\ge2\ \forall j\implies \operatorname{width}\ge2^d.\]

notation.meaning: Reachable values of residual resource coordinate j.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distinguishable dynamic-programming states cannot be merged in an exact decision diagram

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The width lower bound is mathematically plausible under the stated reachability and continuation-distinguishability assumptions, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. No source or inspectable locator supports the decision-diagram reduction claim.

knowledge_statements.title: History-Dependent State Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact diagrams when continuation behavior distinguishes many decision histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At layer \(i\), let \(H_i\) be the reachable decision histories. Declare histories \(h,h'\in H_i\) continuation-equivalent when every common suffix is feasible after \(h\) exactly when it is feasible after \(h'\), and corresponding suffix contributions have the same value. An exact reduced decision diagram requires at least one node for every equivalence class of \(H_i\). Thus, if all \(2^i\) binary histories are reachable and pairwise continuation-distinguishable, the layer width is at least \(2^i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When future feasibility or value distinguishes every reachable history, exact state compression fails and layer width grows with the number of histories.
assumptions_latex: \(H_i\) is the set of reachable histories after \(i\) binary decisions.
Exact nodes may merge only continuation-equivalent histories.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{width}_i\ge |H_i/{\sim}|;\qquad |H_i/{\sim}|=2^i\implies \operatorname{width}_i\ge2^i.\]

notation.meaning: Equivalence by identical feasible continuations and suffix values.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact diagram states correspond to continuation-equivalence classes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The continuation-equivalence lower bound is plausible and matches history-dependent state growth, but no cited source establishes the correspondence between equivalence classes and nodes in an exact reduced diagram.

children.title: Variable-Ordering Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Performance instability caused by order-dependent width, bounds, or mismatch with evolving subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Adverse-Order Width Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Grouped versus interleaved orders for an equality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\ge1\), define \(f_m(x,y)=1\) exactly when \(x_j=y_j\) for all \(j=1,\ldots,m\), with binary variables. Under the grouped order \(x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_m\), after reading all \(x\)-variables an exact ordered binary decision diagram must distinguish the \(2^m\) assignments to \(x\), because each has a different accepting continuation in \(y\). Under the interleaved order \(x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_m,y_m\), equality can be tracked using constant width. Hence an adverse order changes exact width from constant to exponential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For binary-vector equality, grouping both vectors forces exponential width, while interleaving corresponding bits permits constant-width tracking.
assumptions_latex: The diagram is exact, ordered, and reduced.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{width}_{(x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_m)}(f_m)\ge2^m,\qquad \operatorname{width}_{(x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_m,y_m)}(f_m)=O(1).\]

notation.meaning: Equality predicate on two m-bit vectors.
Maximum exact diagram layer width under order pi.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equality is a canonical variable-order separation for ordered decision diagrams

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equality example plausibly demonstrates an exponential-versus-constant width separation, and counterexample is an appropriate role for this leaf. An authoritative OBDD source with a specific locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering-Induced Bound Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of fixed-width relaxation bounds to variable permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximization problem, let \(U_{\pi,W}\) be the upper bound obtained from a relaxed decision diagram of maximum width \(W\) constructed under variable order \(\pi\). Given a set \(\Pi\) of admissible orders and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), ordering-induced bound instability occurs when \(\max_{\pi\in\Pi}U_{\pi,W}-\min_{\pi\in\Pi}U_{\pi,W}>\varepsilon\). Its normalized magnitude is this range divided by \(\max\{1,|z^*|\}\), where \(z^*\) is the exact optimum. The definition reverses upper and lower bounds for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A width-limited bound is ordering-unstable when its range over admissible variable orders exceeds a specified tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Every relaxed diagram supplies a valid upper bound \(U_{\pi,W}\) for the same maximization problem.
\(\Pi\) contains at least two admissible variable orders.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\Delta_W:=\max_{\pi\in\Pi}U_{\pi,W}-\min_{\pi\in\Pi}U_{\pi,W}>\varepsilon.\]

notation.meaning: Relaxed-diagram upper bound under order pi and width limit W.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sensitivity is formalized as variation across admissible orders

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed range is a coherent sensitivity statistic, but the terminology, tolerance criterion, normalization, and claimed minimization reversal are uncited conventions rather than established decision-diagram knowledge.

children.title: Static Variable Orders
children.top_down_role: Fixed compilation orders reused across branching nodes, domain changes, and solver contexts.

knowledge_statements.title: Static Variable Orders
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One global variable permutation shared by all diagram states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) be the decision variables. A static variable order is a permutation \(\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n)\) fixed before diagram construction such that every root-to-terminal path tests or assigns variables only in the sequence \(x_{\pi_1},\ldots,x_{\pi_n}\), possibly skipping variables that are irrelevant on that path. The next eligible variable depends only on the layer index in \(\pi\), not on the state, partial assignment, or search-tree node encountered during construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A static order fixes one global variable sequence; paths may skip variables but cannot adapt the sequence to the current state or subproblem.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite set of decision variables.
Each variable occurs at most once on a root-to-terminal path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\pi\in S_n,\qquad x_{\pi_a}\text{ precedes }x_{\pi_b}\text{ on every path containing both whenever }a<b.\]

notation.meaning: Set of permutations of n indices.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: static ordered decision diagrams use one path-consistent variable permutation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent and definition fits the terminal container, but no inspectable source supports the precise convention allowing skipped variables while preserving one global order.

children.title: Node-Subproblem Drift
children.top_down_role: Changes in active variables, domains, constraints, or objective relevance across the search tree.

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Subproblem Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mismatch between a global order and locally preferred subproblem orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a collection of search nodes, \(V_t\) the variables unfixed at node \(t\), and \(\pi|_{V_t}\) the restriction of a static global order \(\pi\). For each \(t\), let \(\sigma_t\) minimize a stated local diagram criterion \(C_t\), such as exact width or a fixed-width relaxation gap. Node-subproblem drift at \(t\) is \(D_t=C_t(\pi|_{V_t})-C_t(\sigma_t)\). Material drift occurs when \(D_t>	au\) for a prescribed tolerance \(\tau\), and worst-case drift is \(\max_{t\in T}D_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Drift measures how much worse the restricted global order performs than a locally optimal order for a search-node subproblem.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a nonempty collection of subproblems.
Each local criterion \(C_t\) is minimized over permutations of \(V_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D_t:=C_t(\pi|_{V_t})-\min_{\sigma\in S(V_t)}C_t(\sigma);\qquad D_t>\tau\text{ signifies material drift}.\]

notation.meaning: Variables remaining unfixed at search node t.
Local performance loss caused by the static order.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: local order mismatch is expressed as criterion regret

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regret-style quantity is mathematically defined once a criterion is fixed, but “node-subproblem drift” and its threshold are uncited constructions. Different criteria also have incompatible scales, so a decision-diagram source is needed to establish the intended local concept.

children.title: Order-Relevance Failure
children.top_down_role: Width, bound, or compilation degradation when a fixed order no longer matches the current subproblem.

knowledge_statements.title: Order-Relevance Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incompatibility of locally required variable precedences with one static order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each reachable subproblem \(t\), let \(P_t\subseteq V_t\times V_t\) contain the strict precedence pairs \((u,v)\) required for the selected local width or bound guarantee. Form the directed graph \(G=(X,\bigcup_t P_t)\). A single static variable order satisfies all local relevance requirements exactly when \(G\) is acyclic. Consequently, if the union contains a directed cycle, every static order violates at least one locally required precedence; this is order-relevance failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local relevance requirements defeat every static order exactly when their combined precedence graph contains a directed cycle.
assumptions_latex: Each \(P_t\) records strict variable-precedence requirements for subproblem \(t\).
A static order satisfies a requirement only by respecting its directed pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists\pi\text{ respecting every }P_t\iff G\text{ is acyclic};\qquad G\text{ cyclic}\implies\text{static-order relevance failure}.\]

notation.meaning: Required precedence pairs at subproblem t.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: simultaneous precedence constraints admit a linear order exactly when their union is acyclic

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The acyclicity characterization is standard for simultaneous strict precedence constraints, but the claim that these pairs encode the locally required width or bound guarantees is unsupported. A source must establish the decision-diagram interpretation and terminology.

children.title: Approximation Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Weak relaxed bounds or unstable restricted solutions caused by aggregation, discarding, or width allocation.
