knowledge_statements.title: Spurious-Path Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infeasible recombinations introduced by relaxed-state merging.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a relaxed decision diagram for feasible assignment set \(F\), and let \(P(D)\) denote its root-to-terminal assignments. Valid relaxation requires \(F\subseteq P(D)\). The spurious set is \(S(D)=P(D)\setminus F\), with growth factor \(g(D)=|S(D)|/\max\{1,|F|\}\). For a family \((D_n,F_n)\), spurious-path growth is exponential when constants \(c>1\) and \(n_0\) satisfy \(|S(D_n)|\ge c^n\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). Such growth may result from recombining incompatible incoming and outgoing partial paths at merged nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation suffers spurious-path growth when state merging creates exponentially many root-to-terminal assignments that are infeasible in the original problem.
assumptions_latex: \(F_n\subseteq P(D_n)\) for every relaxed diagram in the family.
Root-to-terminal paths encode complete assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S(D_n):=P(D_n)\setminus F_n,\qquad \exists c>1,\ n_0:\ |S(D_n)|\ge c^n\ \forall n\ge n_0.\]

notation.meaning: Assignments represented by root-to-terminal paths of D.
Represented assignments infeasible for the original problem.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: relaxed diagrams may introduce infeasible recombinations while preserving all feasible paths

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The spurious-set construction is coherent and failure_boundary fits the leaf, but the growth factor and exponential-growth convention are uncited. A relaxed-decision-diagram source must support the path-recombination interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Destructive State Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Merging states that have incompatible feasible continuations or values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let states \(p\) and \(q\) at one layer have feasible continuation sets \(C(p)\) and \(C(q)\). Aggregating them into one exact node is lossless only if their continuations are equivalent, including all suffix-value contributions relevant to optimization. If \(C(p)\ne C(q)\), a union aggregation represents a continuation from \(C(p)\triangle C(q)\) after an incompatible prefix and can create a spurious path; an intersection aggregation removes a continuation from \(C(p)\triangle C(q)\) and can delete a feasible path. Thus unequal continuation behavior makes exact aggregation destructive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Merging states with unequal continuation behavior must either admit incompatible paths or discard feasible ones unless extra state information is retained.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) and \(q\) occur at the same layer.
Continuation feasibility and optimization contributions are determined by the diagram state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C(p)\ne C(q)\implies \text{union aggregation may add paths and intersection aggregation may delete paths}.\]

notation.meaning: Feasible suffixes after state p, with relevant suffix values.
Continuations admitted after exactly one of the states.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: lossless exact merging requires continuation equivalence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Continuation inequivalence is relevant to exact merging, but the union/intersection aggregation dichotomy is not defined as a general decision-diagram operation and the “may” conclusions do not fully specify when destruction occurs. An authoritative source is required.

children.title: Premature Loss of Promising Feasible Paths

knowledge_statements.title: Premature Loss of Promising Feasible Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restricted-diagram pruning that removes a prefix of an improving solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a maximization problem and a restricted decision diagram constructed by deleting prefixes to enforce a width limit. Let \(z_D\) be the best terminal-path value retained by the diagram. A deleted prefix \(p\) is promising when it has a feasible completion \(x\) with objective value \(f(x)>z_D\). If such a prefix is removed before a valid upper bound on all of its completions is at most the incumbent, the restriction loses a potentially improving feasible path. In particular, deleting a prefix of every optimal solution makes recovery of the optimum impossible within that diagram.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pruning is premature when it deletes a prefix having a feasible completion better than the diagram’s retained solution, especially a prefix shared by all optima.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a finite maximization problem.
Width enforcement deletes reachable prefixes from a restricted diagram.
\(z_D\) is the best value represented after construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists p,x:\ p\preceq x,\ x\text{ feasible},\ p\text{ deleted},\ f(x)>z_D\implies D\text{ has prematurely lost a promising path}.\]

notation.meaning: Partial assignment p is a prefix of complete assignment x.
Best objective value retained by the restricted diagram.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: restricted diagrams can lose feasible solutions when nodes or prefixes are deleted

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly describes loss of a retained improving completion in a restricted diagram, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. No source with a specific locator supports the restricted-diagram pruning interpretation.

children.title: Width-Budget Misallocation
children.top_down_role: Width assigned to layers or states with limited influence while critical distinctions remain aggregated.

knowledge_statements.title: Width-Budget Misallocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Layerwise capacity assignment under a total node-width budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For layers \(1,\ldots,L\), let \(n_i\) be the width needed to preserve the chosen exactness or bound target, and allocate integer capacities \(w_i\ge1\) under \(\sum_i w_i\le K\). Define waste \(E(w)=\sum_i(w_i-n_i)_+\) and deficit \(D(w)=\sum_i(n_i-w_i)_+\). Width-budget misallocation occurs when \(D(w)>0\) although another allocation \(w'\) with \(\sum_iw'_i\le K\) has \(D(w')=0\), or more generally when transferring capacity from a zero-marginal-gain layer to a positive-marginal-gain layer strictly improves the bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A width budget is misallocated when some layers receive surplus capacity while a feasible redistribution would eliminate deficits or strictly improve the bound.
assumptions_latex: \(K\in\mathbb N\) is a total layer-capacity budget.
Required widths \(n_i\) refer to one fixed exactness or bound target.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D(w)>0\ \land\ \exists w':\sum_iw'_i\le K,\ D(w')=0\implies w\text{ is misallocated}.\]

notation.meaning: Width required at layer i for the selected target.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: layerwise width can be treated as a constrained capacity allocation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The allocation model is internally definable, but a total sum-of-layer-capacities budget is not established here as the width-budget model used by decision diagrams. The alternative marginal-gain clause also lacks a defined bound function.

children.title: Bound-Improvement Plateaus
children.top_down_role: Width increases that yield negligible improvement in relaxation strength or objective bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Improvement Plateaus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intervals of increasing width with no relaxation-bound improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximization problem, let \(U(W)\) be the valid upper bound produced by a nested family of relaxed decision diagrams with width limit \(W\), where increasing width cannot worsen the bound, so \(U(W+1)\le U(W)\). A bound-improvement plateau on integers \([W_1,W_2]\), with \(W_1<W_2\), occurs when \(U(W)=U(W_1)\) for every \(W_1\le W\le W_2\). The plateau is nonexact when this common value exceeds the optimum \(z^*\); additional width in that interval then consumes capacity without tightening the bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A plateau is a range of larger width limits producing the same relaxation bound; it is nonexact when that bound remains above the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(U(W)\) is a valid upper bound for one fixed maximization problem.
The diagram family is nested so that \(U(W+1)\le U(W)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[U(W_1)=\cdots=U(W_2)>z^*\implies [W_1,W_2]\text{ is a nonexact bound-improvement plateau}.\]

notation.meaning: Relaxed-diagram upper bound at width limit W.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a plateau is constancy of a monotone width-indexed bound sequence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The plateau condition is mathematically coherent and condition fits the terminal container. However, monotonicity requires the asserted nested construction and is not automatic for arbitrary width-limited diagram heuristics; an authoritative source and locator are required.

children.title: Layerwise Bottleneck Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where a small set of layers, states, or merge decisions controls attainable bound quality.

assumptions_latex: The exact layered decision diagram has state sets \(S_0,\ldots,S_n\), and every exact representation preserves all feasible root-to-terminal paths.
The imposed layer-width limits are \(w_0,\ldots,w_n\in\mathbb{N}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(|S_k|>w_k\) for some layer \(k\), no exact diagram satisfying the width limits exists without changing the state encoding or variable order.

notation.meaning: Exact reachable state set at layer k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact layerwise width saturation under a fixed state encoding and variable order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a state encoding and variable order for a layered decision diagram. Let \(S_k\) be the set of pairwise nonequivalent reachable states after layer \(k\), where two states are equivalent exactly when they admit identical feasible continuations with identical continuation values. Under layer limits \(w_k\), a bottleneck occurs at layer \(k\) when \(|S_k|>w_k\). Then every diagram respecting those limits must merge nonequivalent states or delete feasible continuations at that layer; consequently it cannot remain an exact representation of both feasibility and continuation value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A layer whose number of distinct continuation states exceeds its width budget forces deletion or inexact merging, so the fixed diagram representation cannot remain exact.
knowledge_statements.title: Layerwise Bottleneck Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the fixed-encoding bottleneck claim is plausible. However, no citation supports the continuation-equivalence convention or the assertion that every exact diagram must realize all stated equivalence classes distinctly.

children.title: Model-Solver Interface Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits caused by unsuitable state models, objective encodings, continuous state, or integration overhead.

assumptions_latex: A layered diagram assigns each partial decision sequence \(p\) a state \(\sigma(p)\).
Exact optimization requires preservation of both feasible continuations and their objective contributions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\sigma(p)=\sigma(q)\) but \(\mathcal{C}(p)\neq\mathcal{C}(q)\), then the state representation is insufficient for exact optimization.

notation.meaning: State assigned to a partial decision sequence
Set of feasible continuation and incremental-value pairs after p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: State sufficiency is characterized by equality of feasible continuation-value information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each partial decision sequence \(p\), let \(\mathcal{C}(p)\) contain every pair consisting of a feasible completion and its incremental objective value after \(p\). A state map \(\sigma\) is sufficient for exact decision-diagram optimization only if \(\sigma(p)=\sigma(q)\) implies \(\mathcal{C}(p)=\mathcal{C}(q)\). Thus, if two partial sequences share a diagram state while their continuation sets or continuation values differ, subsequent arcs cannot represent both subproblems exactly; at least one encoded feasibility or objective value is incorrect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state encoding is insufficient when it merges partial decisions having different feasible completions or different continuation values, preventing exact optimization.
knowledge_statements.title: Insufficient State Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf. A decision-diagram source is required to confirm that the defined continuation-pair set is the necessary state-sufficiency criterion under the intended treatment of incoming path costs and shared suffix structure.

assumptions_latex: Each root-to-terminal path \(P\) represents a feasible solution \(x(P)\).
The solver optimizes the encoded path value \(g(P)\), whereas the intended objective is \(f(x(P))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact objective optimization requires \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{P}g(P)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{P}f(x(P))\); failure of this equality is an objective-encoding mismatch.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mismatch concerns optimizer preservation, not merely equality of numerical objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{P}\) be the feasible root-to-terminal paths of a decision diagram. Path \(P\in\mathcal{P}\) represents solution \(x(P)\), but the solver minimizes an encoded value \(g(P)\). The encoding is optimization-correct precisely when \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathcal{P}} g(P)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathcal{P}} f(x(P))\). An objective-encoding mismatch occurs when this equality fails, including when omitted history-dependent terms assign two paths an encoded ordering opposite to their ordering under the intended objective \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective mismatch occurs when minimizing encoded path costs selects different paths from minimizing the intended objective over the represented solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Encoding Mismatch

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but no source establishes optimizer-set equality as the intended correctness criterion. This criterion can be stronger than preservation of optimal represented solutions or optimal value when paths are nonunique or ties differ.

assumptions_latex: The continuous state lies in a metric space \((X,d)\) and is replaced by a finite quantization map \(Q:X\to G\).
The continuation value \(V:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The statewise value loss satisfies \(|V(x)-V(Q(x))|\leq L\delta\), where \(\delta=\sup_{x\in X}d(x,Q(x))\); exactness is not guaranteed when \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite quantization with a Lipschitz continuation-value bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be the continuous state space and let \(Q:X\to G\) map states to a finite grid \(G\). Define \(\delta=\sup_{x\in X}d(x,Q(x))\). If the exact continuation value \(V\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then \(|V(x)-V(Q(x))|\leq L\delta\) for every \(x\in X\). Hence a decision diagram using only quantized states may incur positive value loss whenever \(\delta>0\); without additional invariance ensuring \(V(x)=V(Q(x))\), discretization alone does not preserve exact optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quantizing continuous states can change continuation values by at most the Lipschitz constant times grid radius, but positive grid radius does not ensure exactness.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-State Discretization Loss

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the formula requires an unstated inclusion or embedding of G in X so that d(x,Q(x)) and V(Q(x)) are defined. A source is also needed to justify interpreting the pointwise Lipschitz deviation as decision-diagram optimization loss.

children.title: Compilation Overhead
children.top_down_role: Time, memory, allocation, and preprocessing burden from constructing or refining solver-facing diagrams.

assumptions_latex: A compiler constructs a layered diagram with \(N\) nodes and \(M\) arcs.
Creating each node and arc takes constant amortized time and stored metadata has constant size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compilation requires \(O(N+M)\) time and \(O(N+M)\) storage, in addition to the subsequent optimization cost.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive construction cost under a constant-amortized explicit-graph model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider explicit compilation of a layered decision diagram containing \(N\) nodes and \(M\) arcs. Under a unit-cost RAM model in which state hashing, node insertion, arc insertion, and constant-size metadata operations take constant amortized time, materializing the diagram requires \(O(N+M)\) time and \(O(N+M)\) storage. Moreover, any compiler that explicitly emits every node and arc requires \(\Omega(N+M)\) output operations. Thus compilation contributes \(\Theta(N+M)\) work in this model before any downstream path or relaxation optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicitly materializing a diagram has linear time and storage overhead in its nodes and arcs under constant-amortized construction operations.
knowledge_statements.title: Compilation Overhead

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the overhead leaf. The conditional output-sensitive estimate is plausible, but no implementation or algorithm source supports the constant-amortized operations or the claimed Theta work for the intended compiler.

children.title: Solver-Synchronization Overhead
children.top_down_role: Cost of exchanging domains, bounds, incumbents, cuts, and validity information with solver components.

assumptions_latex: The compiled diagram contains \(N\) nodes and \(M\) arcs.
Each synchronization round transmits \(u_r\) changed records and scans \(s_r\) diagram records.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Across \(R\) rounds, synchronization work is \(O\!\left(\sum_{r=1}^{R}(u_r+s_r)\right)\), becoming \(O(R(N+M))\) when every round scans the full diagram.

notation.meaning: Changed records transmitted in round r
Diagram records scanned in round r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Record-level synchronization cost between an explicit diagram and an iterative solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a solver performs \(R\) synchronization rounds with a compiled decision diagram. In round \(r\), let \(u_r\) be the number of changed records transmitted and \(s_r\) the number of records inspected to identify or apply changes. Under constant-time record processing, total synchronization work is \(O\!\left(\sum_{r=1}^{R}(u_r+s_r)\right)\). If the interface cannot identify changes incrementally and scans all \(N+M\) node and arc records each round, this becomes \(O(R(N+M))\), even when each \(u_r\) is small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synchronization cost accumulates over transferred and scanned records; full-diagram scans in every solver round can multiply overhead by the number of rounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver-Synchronization Overhead

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the overhead leaf, but the record introduces an interface-specific accounting model without evidence that synchronization consists exactly of the counted transfers and scans or that full scans occur in the stated regime.

children.title: Recompilation Trigger Costs
children.top_down_role: Overhead caused by frequent domain changes, search transitions, model updates, or invalidated diagram caches.

assumptions_latex: There are \(T\) model updates and update \(t\) invalidates a compiled subdiagram of size \(N_t+M_t\).
Recompilation explicitly reconstructs every invalidated node and arc with constant amortized work per record.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Total recompilation work is \(\Theta\!\left(\sum_{t\in I}(N_t+M_t)\right)\), where \(I\) is the set of updates that trigger invalidation.

notation.meaning: Invalidated node and arc counts at update t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive cost of reconstructing invalidated explicit subdiagrams after model updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,T\}\) be the updates whose parameter, constraint, or ordering changes invalidate compiled structure. If update \(t\in I\) forces explicit reconstruction of a subdiagram with \(N_t\) nodes and \(M_t\) arcs, and each record costs constant amortized time to rebuild, then cumulative recompilation work is \(\Theta\!\left(\sum_{t\in I}(N_t+M_t)\right)\). Consequently, frequent globally invalidating updates yield \(\Theta(T(N+M))\) work when \(N_t=N\) and \(M_t=M\) for every update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recompilation cost sums the sizes of invalidated subdiagrams; globally invalidating every update can multiply full compilation cost by the update count.
knowledge_statements.title: Recompilation Trigger Costs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the leaf. A source is needed for the invalidation and reuse model, and constant amortized rebuild time alone ordinarily supplies an upper bound unless explicit emission or another lower-bound assumption is stated.
